articles.title: Fim da 6x1: relator lê parecer; presidente da CCJ concede vista de uma hora após pedido da oposição | G1
articles.standfirst: Texto estabelece duas folgas por semana e redução de 44 para 40 horas por semana em até 14 meses. Parlamentares de oposição ao governo Lula queriam mais tempo para análise do relatório de Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), que mantém texto aprovado pela Câmara.
articles.summary: Texto estabelece duas folgas por semana e redução de 44 para 40 horas por semana em até 14 meses. Parlamentares de oposição ao governo Lula queriam mais tempo para análise do relatório de Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), que mantém texto aprovado pela Câmara.
articles.body:
O presidente da Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado , Otto Alencar (PSD-BA), concedeu nesta quarta-feira (2) vista de uma hora para análise do relatório sobre o fim da escala 6x1 pelos integrantes do colegiado.

Otto Alencar atendeu, parcialmente, a um pedido de parlamentares da oposição ao governo Lula, que defendiam um prazo maior para a análise do relatório. O parecer foi lido nesta quarta pelo senador Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), relator do tema no Senado.

Após o prazo de uma hora de vista, que se encerra às 14h47, a CCJ pode iniciar a votação da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que acaba com a escala de trabalho 6x1. O texto prevê a redução da jornada de trabalho de 44 horas para 40 horas por semana em até 14 meses.

A proposta foi pautada na comissão, após ser destravada pelo presidente da Casa, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP) , que se reaproximou do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) nas últimas semanas.

🔎A CCJ é a principal comissão do Congresso, e funciona como uma 'luz verde' para qualquer projeto que tramita no Legislativo. O colegiado consegue controlar o ritmo e dar peso de validação a uma matéria para ser analisada pelo plenário. É a comissão mais estratégica, que pode interromper previamente determinados projetos.

No relatório, o senador Omar Aziz não fez alterações no texto aprovado pela Câmara dos Deputados.

A Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) do fim da 6x1 estipula uma jornada semanal de 40 horas de trabalho – atualmente, são 44 horas. Com a nova escala, seriam mantidos os limites de 8 horas diárias de trabalho.

A grande mudança é garantir que os trabalhadores tenham dois dias de descanso semanal sem a possibilidade de redução salarial. Preferencialmente, um desses dias deve ser o domingo.

Aziz manteve essas regras em seu parecer. O senador também não fez alterações no período de transição. Se aprovada, a PEC deve seguir a seguinte cronologia:

em dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 42 horas, com dois dias de repouso semanal;

em um ano, redução da jornada semanal para 40 horas.

O fim da escala 6x1, com garantia de ao menos duas folgas semanais, preferencialmente aos domingos, entrará em vigor 60 dias após a promulgação do texto.

Em seu relatório, o parlamentar do PSD defendeu a redução da carga de trabalho. O senador chama a atenção para o fato de que as 44 horas semanais estão em vigor há 30 anos.

E, segundo dados do Instituto de Pesquisa Econômica Aplicada (Ipea) a 6x1 afeta mais os trabalhadores de menor renda e menor escolaridade.

"A jornada prolongada não é, portanto, fenômeno neutramente distribuído na estrutura produtiva: recai de modo desproporcional sobre os trabalhadores de menor renda e menor escolaridade. Reduzi-la é, nessa exata medida, providência de justiça distributiva, e não apenas de política laboral", afirmou Aziz.

articles.summary: Pesquisa Quaest contratada pela Globo mostra que 42% da população considera o presidente Lula mais moderado que o PT, superando numericamente a percepção contrária de 39%.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (2) mostra a opinião dos eleitores sobre Flávio e a família Bolsonaro: 44% acreditam que o candidato do PL à Presidência da República não é mais moderado do que a família, contra 37% que pensam que Flávio Bolsonaro é mais moderado . Outros 19% não sabem ou não responderam.

A diferença, no entanto, recuou de 25 para 7 pontos percentuais. No último levantamento, divulgado pela Quaest em julho, 54% diziam que Flávio não era mais moderado do que a família Bolsonaro, contra 29% que o consideravam mais moderado.

O candidato à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), se reúne na manhã deste domingo (30), em um hotel de São Paulo, com o ministro da Justiça e Segurança Pública de El Salvador, Gustavo Villatoro. — Foto: ALOISIO MAURICIO/FOTOARENA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

articles.title: Pesquisa Quaest: Propostas definem voto de 45% para presidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Ideologia do candidato aparece em segundo lugar, com 17%, e desempenho nos debates na TV vem em seguida, com 14%. Levantamento mostra ainda que 37% dizem estar muito interessados na eleição deste ano. Pesquisa divulgada nesta quarta-feira (2) foi encomendada pelo jornal O Globo e pela Globo.
articles.summary: Ideologia do candidato aparece em segundo lugar, com 17%, e desempenho nos debates na TV vem em seguida, com 14%.
articles.body:
As propostas dos candidatos são o critério mais citado pelos eleitores para definir o voto para presidente, segundo pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (2). O item foi apontado por 45% dos entrevistados.

O levantamento foi encomendado pelo jornal O Globo e pela Globo.

A pergunta feita aos entrevistados foi: "Dentre essas opções, qual é a mais importante para você definir o seu voto para presidente?".

Em segundo lugar aparece a ideologia do candidato, com 17%. O desempenho nos debates na TV vem em seguida, com 14%, e a opinião de amigos, familiares e colegas soma 6%.

As propagandas em rádio e TV foram citadas por 3%, o apoio de outros políticos, por 2% e o apoio de famosos ou celebridades, por 1%. Outros critérios somam 3%, e 9% não souberam ou não quiseram responder.

Opinião de amigos, familiares e colegas: 6%

O que mais pesa na decisão de voto para presidente — Foto: Arte/g1

O peso das propostas cresce conforme a escolaridade. Entre os eleitores com ensino superior, 58% apontam as propostas como critério principal. No ensino médio, são 49%, e entre os que têm ensino fundamental, 34%.

O desempenho nos debates na TV segue o caminho inverso: 17% entre os de ensino fundamental, 14% no ensino médio e 8% entre os de ensino superior. A opinião de amigos, familiares e colegas também é mais citada na base da escala de escolaridade — 8% no fundamental, contra 2% no superior.

A ideologia do candidato é citada por 23% dos eleitores com ensino superior e por 14% dos que têm ensino fundamental.

Por faixa etária, as propostas são apontadas por 48% dos eleitores de 16 a 34 anos e por 46% dos de 35 a 59 anos. Entre os de 60 anos ou mais, o índice é de 35%. A ideologia do candidato tem variação menor entre as faixas: 18% de 16 a 34 anos, 17% de 35 a 59 e 16% entre os de 60 anos ou mais.

Por renda familiar, as propostas são citadas por 47% dos eleitores com renda acima de 5 salários mínimos, 46% na faixa de 2 a 5 salários e 39% entre os que têm até 2 salários mínimos. A ideologia aparece com 21% no topo da escala de renda e 12% na base.

Também por identificação política, as propostas são o critério mais citado em todos os grupos. O índice é de 50% entre os que se declaram de direita não bolsonarista, 45% entre bolsonaristas, 44% entre independentes, e 43% entre lulistas e entre eleitores de esquerda não lulista.

A ideologia do candidato é citada por 22% da direita não bolsonarista, 20% da esquerda não lulista, 20% dos bolsonaristas, 14% dos independentes e 11% dos lulistas.

Por região, as propostas são citadas por 48% no Sul, 44% no Centro-Oeste e Norte, 43% no Sudeste e 42% no Nordeste.

A pesquisa também mediu o interesse dos eleitores na disputa deste ano. Dos entrevistados, 37% dizem estar muito interessados. Eram 36% na rodada de 14 de agosto.

Outros 40% se declaram pouco interessados, ante 42% na pesquisa anterior. Os que dizem não ter interesse na eleição somam 22%, contra 21% no levantamento de agosto.

Interesse na eleição presidencial — Foto: Arte/g1

O interesse na eleição varia conforme a identificação política. Entre os lulistas, 50% dizem estar muito interessados. Entre bolsonaristas, são 45%. Na esquerda não lulista, 40%, e na direita não bolsonarista, 39%.

Entre os que se declaram independentes, 24% dizem estar muito interessados e 33% afirmam não ter interesse na eleição.

O levantamento mostra ainda que 71% dos eleitores afirmam que a escolha de voto é definitiva, e 29% dizem que ainda pode mudar. Em março, os que consideravam o voto definido eram 56%.

A Quaest, contratada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo, entrevistou 2.004 eleitores de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 30 de agosto e 1º de setembro. A margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais para mais ou para menos, com nível de confiança de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral como BR-07065/2026.

articles.title: Câmara dos Deputados aprova indicação, e Rodrigo Pacheco será ministro do TCU | G1
articles.standfirst: Pacheco foi apadrinhado pelo presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), que acelerou o processo para sua aprovação após a abertura de uma vaga após a saída antecipada do ministro Bruno Dantas.
articles.summary: Pacheco foi apadrinhado pelo presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), que acelerou o processo para sua aprovação após a abertura de uma vaga após a saída antecipada do ministro Bruno Dantas.
articles.body:
A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta quarta-feira (2) a indicação do senador Rodrigo Pacheco (PSB-MG), de 49 anos, para o cargo de ministro do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU).

Ele foi aprovado com o placar de 404 votos favoráveis a 61 . Indicação será promulgada pelo Congresso.

O nome de Pacheco havia sido aprovado também pelo Senado nessa terça-feira (1), em uma votação relâmpago, aprovada direto pelo plenário da Casa, sem análise da Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos (CAE).

O nome de Pacheco foi apadrinhado pelo presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), que acelerou o processo para sua aprovação após a abertura de uma vaga após a saída antecipada do ministro Bruno Dantas.

O senador Rodrigo Pacheco (PSD-MG). — Foto: Edilson Rodrigues/Agência Senado

Alcolumbre defendia a indicação de Rodrigo Pacheco para uma vaga no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), aberta com a aposentadoria do ministro Luís Roberto Barroso.

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), no entanto, optou por indicar o advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias, que acabou rejeitado pelo Senado.

Após a derrota do indicado, Lula se afastou politicamente de Alcolumbre por considerar que o presidente do Senado atuou para inviabilizar a aprovação de Messias. Recentemente, porém, os dois retomaram o diálogo.

A aproximação ocorre em um momento em que o governo busca apoio para avançar com pautas consideradas prioritárias no Congresso durante o ano eleitoral, entre elas as propostas de emenda à Constituição (PECs) que tratam do fim da escala 6x1 e da segurança pública, além da medida provisória que extingue a chamada taxa das blusinhas.

Relator da indicação, o deputado federal Aécio Neves (PSDB-MG) afirmou que Pacheco está apto, "portanto, a exercer não apenas o posto de Ministro do Tribunal de Contas da União, mas qualquer cargo no cume da cordilheira estatal que exija notório saber jurídico e administrativo, reputação ilibada, idoneidade moral inatacável e compromisso com a democracia".

"O equilíbrio e moderação nata e notórias de Rodrigo Pacheco permitirão que o momento em que tantas inquietudes passam o país, ele será aberto ao diálogo, equilíbrio e moderação tão necessárias aos dias de hoje", prosseguiu o relator.

Rodrigo Otávio Soares Pacheco é advogado. É graduado em Direito pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Minas Gerais.

Iniciou a trajetória política como deputado federal por Minas Gerais. Na Câmara, chegou a presidir a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça e de Cidadania, antes de ser eleito senador nas eleições de 2018.

Chegou ao comando do Senado em fevereiro de 2021 com ampla coalizão partidária, reelegendo-se posteriormente para o biênio seguinte.

Ao longo da presidência do Legislativo, consolidou-se como articulador moderado e institucional, exercendo papel de interlocução entre os poderes Executivo e Judiciário e posicionando-se em defesa dos ritos democráticos.

Passou por legendas como MDB e DEM, migrou para o PSD e, posteriormente, para o PSB.

Teve seu nome cotado e articulado por aliados para a disputa ao governo de Minas Gerais. Contudo, confirmou publicamente a desistência de concorrer ao estado, indicando também sua intenção de encerrar a carreira política eletiva ao fim do mandato como senador.

articles.title: 'Taxa das blusinhas': comissão analisa relatório para acabar com imposto; Motta convoca sessão para votar MP nesta quarta | G1
articles.standfirst: A MP vence, ou seja, deixa de valer em 8 de setembro. Para que o imposto não seja retomado, o texto precisa ser analisado pelo Congresso antes disso. O objetivo é finalizar a votação no Congresso ainda nesta semana.
articles.summary: A MP vence, ou seja, deixa de valer em 8 de setembro. Para que o imposto não seja retomado, o texto precisa ser analisado pelo Congresso antes disso. O objetivo é finalizar a votação no Congresso ainda nesta semana.
articles.body:
A Comissão Mista para análise da MP do fim da taxa das blusinhas começou a analisar, nesta terça-feira (2), o parecer para acabar com o imposto em compras internacionais de até US$ 50 .

Após essa etapa, o texto seguirá para votação no plenário da Câmara. O presidente da Casa, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), já convocou uma sessão, prevista para iniciar às 14h, com essa finalidade .

Depois de chegar perto de caducar, a MP da taxa das blusinhas foi destravada no Congresso por um acordo entre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e os presidentes da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), e do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP). Em um almoço na quarta-feira (26), eles anunciaram que o tema seria votado.

"Eu faço compromisso, como foi com Motta, com o Brasil, que precisa dessa matéria em vigência, que na semana que vem, no tempo curto de esforço concentrado, vamos deliberar, para sancionar e virar lei, para milhões de brasileiros e terem qualidade de vida melhor", declarou Alcolumbre.

Depois disso, dois aliados do presidente Lula foram escolhidos para comandar a comissão sobre o tema: o deputado Reginaldo Lopes (PT-MG) e a senadora Leila Barros (PDT-DF).

articles.title: Leonardo DiCaprio se reúne com Lula e Janja no Planalto hoje | G1
articles.standfirst: Encontro começou por volta das 13h e, conforme a agenda de Janja, o ator está acompanhado de representantes da Re:wild uma organização ambiental que ajudou a fundar.
articles.summary: O ator Leonardo DiCaprio e a organização Re:wild discutem a preservação ambiental com o presidente Lula e a primeira-dama Janja em reunião no Palácio do Planalto.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) e a primeira-dama, Janja da Silva, receberam nesta quarta-feira (2) o ator e ambientalista Leonardo DiCaprio no Palácio do Planalto.

O encontro iniciou por volta das 13h e, conforme a agenda de Janja, o ator está acompanhado de representantes da Re:wild, uma organização ambiental global sem fins lucrativos, fundada em 2021 com a participação de DiCaprio, com foco na restauração ecológica.

🔎A Re:wild, segundo a própria organização, também atua em parceria com comunidades indígenas, governos e cientistas para a recuperação de ecossistemas e proteção de espécies ameaçadas de extinção.

DiCaprio foi alvo de ataques de Bolsonaro

Em 2019, uma declaração do então presidente Jair Bolsonaro sobre Leonardo DiCaprio repercutiu internacionalmente.

"Quando eu falei que há suspeitas de ONGs, o que a imprensa fez comigo? Agora, o Leonardo DiCaprio é um cara legal, não é? Dando dinheiro para tacar fogo na Amazônia", disse Bolsonaro a apoiadores no Palácio da Alvorada em novembro de 2019.

Bolsonaro deu a declaração no contexto da prisão de quatro brigadistas na região de Alter do Chão, no Pará, que foram presos pela Polícia Civil do estado por suspeita de atear fogo na floresta com a finalidade de obter doações ( relembre no vídeo acima ).

As prisões foram criticadas por entidades ambientalistas que apoiavam a atividade de brigadistas.

Na oportunidade, o Ministério Público do Pará disse que não havia indícios do envolvimento de brigadistas e que investigava a ação de grileiros em Alter do Chão . O chefe da investigação da Polícia Civil foi afastado e a Justiça do Pará determinou a soltura dos brigadistas.

À época, as declarações de Bolsonaro repercutiram negativamente fora do país. Os jornais americanos "Washington Post" e "New York Times" destacaram que o presidente do Brasil criticou DiCaprio após incêndios na Amazônia e afirmaram que Bolsonaro não ofereceu nenhuma prova. O britânico "The Guardian" diz que Bolsonaro acusou falsamente o ator de ter pago pelos incêndios.

articles.summary: Renan Santos aparece com 3%, e Caiado e Zema têm 1% cada. Pesquisa divulgada nesta quarta-feira (2) foi encomendada pelo jornal O Globo e pela Globo.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta quarta-feira (2) sobre a eleição presidencial mostra que Lula (PT) lidera com 37%, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) tem 29% e Augusto Cury (Avante) agora é o terceiro colocado, com 10% .

Na sequência, Renan Santos (Missão) tem 3% e Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) e Romeu Zema (Novo), 1% cada. O levantamento foi encomendado pelo jornal O Globo e pela Globo e é o primeiro a ser divulgado após a série de entrevistas com os candidatos à Presidência realizada na semana passada .

O avanço de Cury é explicado pelo bom desempenho entre os eleitores independentes, afirma Felipe Nunes, diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV). "Nesse segmento, o candidato do Avante já alcança 24% e fica numericamente à frente de Lula", diz. Leia a análise de Nunes sobre a pesquisa .

57% dos eleitores de Renan Santos agora admitem trocar de candidato, e 58% dos eleitores de Caiado dizem o mesmo.

articles.title: Golden explains defection on GOP rule: ‘I’m going with the fishermen’
articles.summary: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday explained his choice to split from his party to support a Republican rule governing a series of GOP messaging bills, saying he was “going with the fishermen.” He and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) broke from their Democratic colleagues to advance four bills, with one of the bills being…
articles.body:
Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday explained his choice to split from his party to support a Republican rule governing a series of GOP messaging bills, saying he was “going with the fishermen.”

He and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) broke from their Democratic colleagues to advance four bills , with one of the bills being a resolution to condemn socialism .

The rule also included a bill Golden proposed to provide lobstermen with economic protections as a result of the protections for the North Atlantic right whale, which passed late Tuesday evening.

“I have great empathy for right whales,” Golden told the Substack “ Out of State ” after the vote. “I want to see them survive.”

“But given the reality of what’s going on here, that most of their deaths have nothing to do with Maine lobstermen, if it’s a choice between Maine fishing communities and the right whales, I, as a representative for Maine’s 2nd District, I’m going with the fishermen and the families and the communities that they live in,” he added.

The lawmaker also noted that if he sided with Democrats, he would have felt as though he let the fishermen and lobstermen down and like he turned his “back on them when it mattered.”

Golden said the regulations to protect right whales left lobstermen “terrified” and “unworkable to the point where there would be hard discussions in communities about which families get to keep fishing and which to give it up.” He suggested that the protection could lead fisheries to fail, comparing it to a “mill closure,” and decimate local economies.

“No property tax base, schools closed, everyone moves away –– it’s just devastating,” the Maine Democrat added. “I literally had fishermen telling me that they were contemplating suicide.”

He explained it was a “nonsensical conversation” to defend siding with Democratic leadership by opposing the GOP bills and his own legislation. Voting against the bill he introduced “to help my core constituency” would have been received as “just a bitter betrayal,” he added.

The two Democratic defections effectively salvaged House Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) September agenda, as the bills’ messaging on socialism, environmental protection and Israel could challenge Democrats who are vulnerable to challenges in the November midterm elections.

House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark (Mass.) said after the vote that Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez’s votes “came as a surprise.” Her Bay State colleague, Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), dismissed any notion of party members punishing the two for their votes.

“No, no, no,” he said. “Who are we, the Republicans?”

Gluesenkamp Perez suggested she supported the GOP rule to ensure the lobster bill passed, saying that environmental protections are not assured without “the input of people who make their livelihoods and heritage on the water.”

articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: Trump’s 9/11 tribute to feature massive piece of Ground Zero history at White House
articles.summary: Trump will welcome NYPD first responders and Tunnel to Towers Foundation representatives to the White House to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will host 9/11 first responders and officials at the White House on Sept. 8, where a 21-foot steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center’s South Tower will be displayed, Fox News Digital learned. "President Trump will pay tribute to the American heroes we lost in the tragic Sept. 11 attacks, their beautiful family members and to the acts of heroism that defined that fateful day when the unbreakable spirit of the American people prevailed," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation will bring its "Steel Across America" tour to the White House on Sept. 8, where the 21-foot, 16,900-pound steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center’s South Tower will be displayed on the White House Ellipse. MASSIVE WORLD TRADE CENTER STEEL BEAM ARRIVES AT WEST POINT, UNITING 9/11 HEROES WITH GENERATION SENT TO WAR "The president will stand with first responders to renew our sacred vow that we will never forget – and that the United States of America will always defend our proud, free nation with unyielding resolve," said Wales. Trump and Tunnel to Towers Foundation Chairman and CEO Frank Siller are expected to speak. The president will also attend a ceremony at the Pentagon while Vice President JD Vance will travel to New York City’s World Trade Center site, and other administration officials will represent the White House in Shanksville, Pennsylvania — marking all three locations targeted or affected by the attacks. RETIRED PORT AUTHORITY OFFICERS TELL MAMDANI, HOCHUL TO STAY AWAY FROM GROUND ZERO ON 9/11 Last year, Trump and first lady Melania Trump attended a 9/11 commemoration at the Pentagon and issued a Patriot Day proclamation calling for flags to be flown at half-staff. He later attended a Yankees-Tigers game featuring tributes to the victims in the Bronx, New York City. The steel beam has served as a traveling memorial to the victims and first responders of 9/11, offering pop-up events across 21 states leading up to the anniversary of the tragic day. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS "Never forgetting the sacrifice and bravery of our nation’s heroes, as well as our lost loved ones, is a generational promise that every American can help keep," Tunnel to Towers Foundation Chairman and CEO Frank Siller previously told Fox News Digital. Siller founded the organization in honor of his brother, FDNY firefighter Stephen Siller, who died responding to the attacks. Tunnel to Towers has provided mortgage-free homes to families of fallen service members and first responders while also working to combat veteran homelessness. articles.title: Canadian PM tells Trump to 'stop trying to be tough' in trade fight
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told Americans to "stop trying to be tough" and called U.S. Cabinet secretaries' mockery "beneath their office."
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Americans need to "stop trying to be tough" during the countries' contentious trade negotiations. Speaking to reporters in Ottawa about U.S.-Canadian trade negotiations over automobile tariffs, Carney said, "When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions." "Look, it's not constructive, but that's their democracy," Carney added. TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT After Canada suspended trade talks on Aug. 21, Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario, which is bordered by New York and Canada's Ontario province, to Lake America. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and War Secretary Pete Hegseth also mocked Canada in social media posts, with Bessent writing that Canada could not go "tit-for-tat" with America's economy and Hegseth posting a photo of two female Canadian military members with the caption "this is real." When asked to comment on U.S. Cabinet secretaries mocking the Canadian military, Carney responded, "It's beneath their office." Carney cited both the U.S. posture and its terms in negotiations and barriers to reaching a deal. TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS "The issues with respect to language and culture — enough to not have to deal. The issues Mr. Gray just asked about, with respect to restrictions on future trade deals, restrictions on our sovereignty — enough not to have a deal. Issues with respect to locking in an uncompetitive, trade arrangement in our key industries, automobiles being one of them — enough to not have a trade deal," he continued. "And then the general attitude, and I’ll leave you with this, which I think this is a very important point, is that the attitude of the United States in these discussions and subsequently has been one that, the core Canadian industries either would be subsidiaries effectively of the United States industries or would put in place terms where those industries would be, gradually wound down in Canada and we're not going to of course, we're not going to accept those terms." Trump, following Carney's suspension of negotiations, accused Canada of wanting "the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!" In a post on Truth Social, Trump also said Canada has been taking advantage of the U.S. by charging U.S. farmers tariffs. TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE Carney, for his part, said America's insistence that it have a say over who else Canada trades with was a bridge too far. He also said the U.S. view of the trade relationship was "misguided," adding that on automobiles, the U.S. needs both Canada and Mexico. FEARS OF A CANADIAN TRADE WAR ARE OVERBLOWN. SO FAR, IT’S MORE OF A SKIRMISH "The United States auto industry is made stronger by the Canadian and the Mexican auto industries. And at a time of big, big change in auto, it's important that we work together. That's why I say yes, there is a mutually beneficial deal," he told reporters. Carney did leave the door open for further negotiations. ‘CAPTAIN CANADA’ FIREBRAND UNLOADS ON TRUMP WITH PROFANE ONE-LINER AS TRADE WAR ESCALATES "There were elements of that mutually beneficial deal that we were moving towards, which is why we were still at the table. But we never, viewed that we had that deal. And it diverged towards the end. At some point, maybe it'll converge again," Carney said. He told lawmakers in his country that relations with the U.S. will not "go back to normal any time soon" and said the situation is "a new normal that we have to get adjusted to." TRUMP ALLIES PUSH TO ARM PRESIDENT WITH NEW TARIFF WEAPON TO PUNISH COUNTRIES 'RIPPING OFF' AMERICA Carney, matching a slate of tariffs the U.S. imposed on Canadian goods such as steel and lumber, imposed his own set of tariffs which he said will go "dollar for dollar" with America's tariffs. The Canadian levies are set to take effect on Sept. 8. "Canada was offered the most generous trade deal of any of America’s trading partners despite being overwhelmingly reliant on access to the American economy, which is over 12-times larger than Canada’s economy. Canada rejected that deal to demand continued one-sided access to the American market with no reciprocity. President Trump was given a resounding Election Day mandate to put American workers, farmers, and businesses first, and the Administration will continue to deliver while lowering costs for everyday families," White House Spokesman Kush Desai told Fox News Digital in a statement. articles.title: Talarico’s ‘proud capitalist’ about-face collides with resurfaced call to ‘dismantle’ capitalism
articles.summary: James Talarico once called capitalism "oppressive" and predicted Texas' fossil fuel industry was "not gonna last" in a 2020 Sierra Club Zoom call.
articles.body: The James Talarico campaign says the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas is a "proud capitalist," even though he once described capitalism as an "oppressive system" that needed to be dismantled — and predicted that Texas’ fossil fuel industry was "not gonna last." The remarks, made during a resurfaced 2020 Zoom call with Sierra Club activists, are drawing fresh scrutiny as Talarico faces Republican nominee and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in a Senate race that could help determine control of the chamber. The comments were first reported by CNN early Tuesday and were seized on by Lone Star Liberty PAC, an outside political group aligned with Paxton, and Senate Leadership Fund, a leading super PAC backing Senate Republicans. THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE On the call, Talarico is heard saying that the U.S. was facing a "multi-faceted threat" of a climate, economic and social crisis. After an activist asked how to address the harm suffered by communities of color by climate change, Talarico responded, "I’m so thankful that you asked this question and also thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country." "I think only understanding the ways that all three of those oppressive systems work together are we going to be able to begin the process of dismantling them." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Talarico, during the same forum, forecast that Texas' fossil fuel industry wouldn't last. "We all know that Texas has been a leader in oil and gas, but in many ways that’s like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s. That industry is not gonna last," Talarico said. Asked for comment, Talarico campaign spokesperson J.T. Ennis told Fox News Digital, "James is a proud capitalist and agrees with the majority of Texans that racism, natural disasters, and a billionaire-controlled economy are all problems we need to address." "James has already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, while Ken Paxton has refused to address his comments that the school shooting in Uvalde was ‘God’s plan’ and that Texas’ abortion ban is good for interstate commerce," Ennis added. The Talarico campaign also spotlighted that the state lawmaker had "taken many votes" in support of the oil industry. And the campaign website states that he aims to make sure that Texas "not only maintains, but extends" its energy dominance. WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW The Paxton campaign and Republicans have repeatedly targeted Talarico for past comments he's made on social issues, including his prior suggestion that "God is nonbinary," that he "hates Christianity," and that "there are many more than two biological sexes; in fact, there are six." Talarico, a 37-year-old former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, defeated progressive firebrand and vocal critic of President Donald Trump Rep. Jasmine Crockett in the March Democratic Senate primary. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Paxton, a longtime Trump ally, captured the GOP nomination in late May, after defeating longtime Republican Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff election. The combustible clash between the two Texas titans shaped up as a fight between the Republican establishment and Trump's MAGA and America First supporters. Trump stayed neutral in the intra-party battle until giving Paxton an 11th-hour endorsement. The general election face-off in deep-red Texas between Talarico and Paxton is one of roughly a dozen races that will likely decide if Republicans hold the Senate majority or if Democrats win back control of the chamber. Democrats haven't won a Senate election in Texas in nearly four decades, but they view Paxton as vulnerable because of the slew of scandals and legal problems that have battered him over the past decade. And Paxton is dealing with a messy divorce, with his wife citing "biblical grounds" based on "recent discoveries" in filing last year to end their marriage. Talarico enjoys a large fundraising advantage over Paxton. Meanwhile, the most recent Fox News poll in the Texas Senate showdown, conducted in late July, indicated Talarico holding a slight 51%-48% edge over Paxton among registered voters. articles.title: Jewish Democrats abandon El-Sayed for GOP rival in all-important battleground state
articles.summary: Over 400 Michigan Jewish Democrats signed a letter backing Mike Rogers, but former Rep. Andy Levin claims AIPAC is really driving the effort.
articles.body: More than 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders are backing Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and warning that they feel "threatened and alienated" by leftist candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his political allies. Prominent Democratic donor Rob Orley, a senior advisor for O2 Investments, is among the signatories. He previously donated tens of thousands of dollars to Democratic campaigns, according to FEC campaign filings — but now he and other prominent Jewish leaders are ditching El-Sayed for Republican candidate Mike Rogers. "Many of us have been fiercely supportive of Democratic candidates and principles," a letter signed by Orley and hundreds of others stated. "If El-Sayed were to win the general election in this important swing state, we fear the far-left and anti-Jewish elements in the Democratic Party would become dominant, including in the imminent 2028 presidential race," the letter continues. "We cannot allow him to become the Democratic standard-bearer or Michigan’s senator." Fox News Digital reached out to O2 Investments for comment. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS The letter includes signatures from some of the most prominent members of Michigan's Jewish community, including Robert Gordon, the former president of Temple Israel, the state's largest Jewish congregation, which was the site of an antisemitic attack in March. Shayna Levine, the daughter of the leading rabbi at Temple Israel; David Propis, cantor of Congregation Shaarey Zedek; Laurence Deitch, who served as a University of Michigan regent; and Hannan Lis, a Weight Watchers executive, have also signed the letter declaring that they feel "threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed." But former Rep. Andy Levin, who is Jewish, is claiming that opposition to El-Sayed among Jewish Democrats is a minority view and that his old foe, the American Israel Political Action Committee, is really driving the letter. Levin lost his 2022 primary bid to Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., after AIPAC spent more than $4 million in the primary race against him. "It's not a surprise to me," Levin said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The people I know associated with it are all long-time AIPAC insiders and supporters." Levin added that AIPAC "represents a distinctly minority position about Israel and Palestine within the Jewish community." Levin, who was first elected to Congress in 2018 to replace his late father Sander Levin, gave his endorsement to El-Sayed in November 2025. "I am overwhelmed like literally every day except Shabbat — our sabbath on Saturday — with the incoming I get from Jewish people, young people, middle-aged people, older people, who are so mad about an effort like this and who want to do everything they can to make sure Abdul El-Sayed wins the election on November 3rd, that this U.S. Senate seat stays democratic, and that we do everything we can to save and expand our democracy," Levin continued. "I am very concerned about the movement that is behind Abdul, and for the safety of my community, I don't feel safe in that environment with the people that are standing in support of him," Cherrin told Fox News Digital. "And so, for that, I am very worried about should he be elected what that means for all those that are trying to advance his candidacy." Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who has called Orthodox Jews inbreds and said America deserved 9/11, has been a top surrogate for El-Sayed's campaign. Over the past week, El-Sayed has attempted to distance himself from the social media influencer, suggesting that people focusing on his affiliation with Piker are "missing the boat." Levin, who has condemned Piker's antisemitic falsehoods about the Oct. 7 attack, agreed with El-Sayed that too much focus is on Piker. He then argued that the Democratic National Committee received very little pushback for inviting Piker to stream during the 2024 Democratic National Convention, giving then-Vice President and Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris an opportunity to reach Piker's audience. Piker did not endorse Harris because of the Biden administration's policy in the Gaza war. "So I'm not accepting Hasan Piker, but look in the mirror, sister," Levin said. "When it's a guy named Abdul with a guy named Hasan, you're blowing up about it and covering it massively. When it was not an Arab American or a Muslim who campaigned with him or did whatever Kamala Harris did, literally no one asked her a single question about it." Last month, El-Sayed said he had "no plans" to continue campaigning with Piker. Roslyn Schindler attends Congregation T'chiyah, which is a progressive Reform synagogue that touts its support for Black Lives Matter, and transgender rights, with Levin. A daughter of Holocaust survivors, Schindler has lived in the metro Detroit area for 50 years and taught Holocaust studies at Wayne State University. She shared with Fox News Digital that she has supported El-Sayed well before his primary victory, and that the Democratic Party is in need of a "major shake-up," citing El-Sayed's support for progressive policies like Medicare for All and getting money out of politics. "I am certainly not an anti-Zionist, as many Jews who don't support Abdul think we are, but I am a committed Jew," Schindler told Fox News Digital. "I'm a committed Democrat. I believe that the Democratic Party should be a large tent, so to speak, that includes all members of that party, no matter what their perspective." Fox News Digital asked Schindler for her thoughts on El-Sayed's affiliation with Piker and whether there is a place in the Democratic Party for people who follow his ideology. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER "As a Jew, I certainly don't want anyone to be anti-Semitic. I don't want anyone to be anti-Muslim. I don't want anyone to be anti-LGBTQ, and the list goes on," Schindler said. "Is that realistic? Probably not. Do I want those people to be part of the Democratic Party? It's not really for me to want. It is what it is. They'll either be part of it or they won't." "But I do believe there is enough traction within the Jewish community at large to counter anti-Semitism, and that's across the board," Schindler continued. But Cherrin said the fact that his family has to pass security officers guarding synagogues and temples is evidence to him that the Jewish community at large can't tackle antisemitism by itself. "It's not about AIPAC for me," Cherrin said. "It is about it is about how are we protecting the sanctity of the Jewish community in Michigan and frankly and across the country with all these other races that are out there." "People within the Jewish community, who typically identify as Democrats, don't feel comfortable voting for the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate and are looking for a place to channel their frustration. "As antisemitism rises and Jewish families worry for their safety, it’s critical that we have leaders who will confront hatred — not inflame it," Rogers said in a statement. "That’s where my opponent and I couldn’t be more different." "Abdul El-Sayed fans the flames of antisemitism. We’re fighting to extinguish it," Rogers continued. "We have a chance to protect our Democracy by keeping this U.S. Senate seat democratic and expanding our democracy, by, for the first time, having, uh, electing a Muslim to the U.S. Senate," Levin said. articles.title: Odd that Lake Ontario would be what finally turns the public against Trump
articles.summary: The naysayers might have jumped on the wrong legal bandwagon.
articles.body:
On Thursday, President Trump issued an Executive Order entitled “Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.” In it, Trump asserts that because “the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters” are “within United States territory” and “the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume,” he gets to change the lake’s historic name unilaterally.

But approximately 55 percent of Lake Ontario’s surface area is in Canada, with the official international boundary running through the middle.

According to a YouGov poll, only 19 percent of Americans support Trump’s maneuver, an obviously petty snub of our friendly neighbor to the north. Before declaring the negative polling “better late than never,” however, it is worth pointing out that the naysayers might have jumped on the wrong legal bandwagon. This is one executive order that finds Trump on relatively legitimate legal footing — which makes the public outrage almost tragic.

The same poll puts Trump’s overall approval rating at 36 percent. The public seems more disturbed about his renaming of Lake Ontario than, say, the 18 U.S. service members killed and 756 wounded in Trump’s senseless Iran war; the 66,000 people currently in immigration detention camps, over 70 percent of whom have no criminal convictions ; the roughly 0.2 to 0.4-point rise in inflation due to Trump’s ongoing tariffs; his astonishingly corrupt pay-to-play engagements with ultra-wealthy individuals, corporations, special interests, and foreign governments; his recent lowering of standards for FBI recruits to tolerate stealing, the hiring of sex workers, and even bestiality; the appearance of his name over 38,000 times in the Epstein files, which still have not been released in their entirety despite a congressional mandate; and the staggering wealth Trump and his unelected family members have accumulated since he retook office.

The list of things to be upset about is endless. The renaming of Lake Ontario amounts to dust on the national windshield by comparison.

Trump cites a specific federal law to justify the renaming. That law broadly gives the Secretary of the Interior, “conjointly with the Board on Geographic Names,” authority to “provide for uniformity in geographic nomenclature and orthography throughout the federal government.” One section goes on to state that the joint agencies’ naming decisions must be “designed to serve the interests of the federal government and the general public” and “give full consideration to the specific interests of particular federal and state agencies.”

Established in 1890, the Board of Geographic Names has members from numerous federal agencies, including the the CIA, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Homeland Security and the so-called Department of War — another nominal reinvention of Trump, who also renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.”

Cornell law professor Michael Dorf has thoughtfully argued that the law requires more than just following Trump’s orders — that unless Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the Board of Geographic Names actually undertake an inquiry into whether renaming Lake Ontario is in the interests of the federal government and the general public, Burgum’s actions to implement the executive order are illegal.

As Dorf points out, however, Trump and Burgum already thwarted these criteria when they avowedly changed the Gulf of Mexico’s name to the Gulf of America. Since then, the Trump-friendly majority on the Supreme Court has overruled a 90-year-old precedent allowing Congress to establish agency independence from presidents by requiring that certain officials be fired only “for cause” rather than for purely political reasons.

The court thereby stripped that constitutional power from Congress. Except for members of the Federal Reserve Board — an exception that is intellectually disingenuous as a matter of Article II of the Constitution — presidents now have unfettered power over agency heads and thus, in effect, everything they do, lest they be fired for insubordination. In 2024, the same court gave presidents virtually limitless legal immunity from liability for the commission of crimes using the massive powers of the office.

It is therefore folly to suggest that Burgum will think independently about whether Lake Ontario’s name after Trump’s unequivocal executive order. Although Burgum could face a civil lawsuit for failing to comply with the technical procedural requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act in implementing the order, the potential impact of such litigation, even if successful, is almost comically anemic.

The leader of the Seneca Nation, President J. Conrad Seneca, has also argued that Trump’s action is barred by the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua, which the U.S. entered into with a group of six tribal nations called the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. But Trump already managed to bypass Congress in violation of the Constitution when he attacked Iran, to kidnap the sovereign president of Venezuela and his wife from their bedchamber in defiance of international law, and to impose new tariffs on foreign nations despite a Supreme Court ruling confirming that the constitutional powers over tariffs belongs exclusively to Congress.

Over 100 international law experts have even gone so far as to suggest that Trump has engaged in war crimes. Complaining about an historic tribal treaty seems downright quaint.

The rule of law is over in America. If it takes the end of Lake Ontario for the American people to wake up to that reality and demand a reckoning, so be it. The Canadian people are with us.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: $1 gold Trump coins go on sale Sept. 2
articles.summary: Trump is the first living person in more than a century to appear on currency.
articles.body:
The United States Mint will soon begin selling a $1 gold coin emblazoned with President Donald Trump 's face, making him the first living person featured on American currency in more than a century.

The coins go on sale Sept. 2 at 12 p.m. ET. Collectors can purchase 100 coins for $154.50 or a roll of 25 for $61.00. Dispersed among the bags and rolls are 250,000 coins pressed on the Fourth of July , with a "July 4" privy mark, the Treasury said in a news release.

Featuring Trump's official White House portrait, the coins were designed to commemorate the country's 250 th anniversary.

They are the first released in a slate of Trump-adorned currency announced by the Treasury. The agency has also proposed a $250 bill and 24K gold commemorative coin with the president's image.

Some Democrats and coin collectors have questioned the legality of the coins , pointing to a federal law allowing "only the portrait of a deceased individual" to appear on U.S. currency and securities.

The Treasury, however, has pointed to a 2020 law allowing it to mint a $1 coin honoring the nation's semiquincentennial for one year.

George Washington refused to have his image printed on currency during his lifetime, believing it was " monarchical. "

Trump's naming campaign from the Kennedy Center to Trump RX

From Lake America to buildings and institutions bearing Trump's name, see the places, landmarks and public spaces tied to the president's branding campaign. Pictured here, a map labeling Lake Ontario as " Lake America " is displayed as President Donald Trump signs an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" on Aug. 27, 2026, amid an ongoing trade war between the U.S. and Canada. See what Trump has renamed or attached his name to.

President Calvin Coolidge was the last and only other sitting executive to appear on currency. In 1926, for the country's 150 th anniversary, the Treasury issued a half-dollar featuring Coolidge and George Washington.

Neither the $1 gold coin nor the 24K gold commemorative coin received approval from the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, a nonpartisan group created by Congress to advise the treasury on coin designs. That committee declined to review both coins, arguing that putting a sitting president on currency was against the country's founding principles.

While described as "gold coins," the $1 tokens don't contain any precious metals. Rather, the Treasury said they have a "gold-like finish."

Karissa Waddick covers America's 250th anniversary, looking at how historical events have shaped our nation. She can be reached at kwaddick@usatoday.com.

articles.title: Holiday travel is months away. Why an expert says you should book flights now
articles.summary: Sure, it’s only September, but if you’re planning to travel for the holidays, now may be the best time to book.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – It’s only barely September, but your mind may already be drifting toward traveling for the holidays. (There are about 85 days to Thanksgiving, and just over 110 until Christmas.)

While they may feel far off, you may want to book your flights now, an expert warns.

The advice has long been that, if you are flying domestically, the best time to buy your airfare is a month or two in advance. For international flights, you may want to look three to six months ahead of time.

That advice is outdated this year, Clint Henderson, travel expert for The Points Guy, told Nexstar. The war in Iran has caused jet fuel prices to spike, which has, in turn, caused airlines to raise ticket prices and baggage fees , and even impose fuel surcharges .

Though Chris Sununu, the CEO of Airlines for America, told Nexstar’s NewsNation that he doesn’t believe airfare will “go up significantly,” Henderson said prices are expected to continue to rise.

Already, an analysis by The Points Guy and Points Path has found that Thanksgiving and Christmas flights are up 13% and 18%, respectively, over last year.

Because of this, it’s recommended that you “book holiday travel ASAP,” Henderson explained.

“You probably have until Labor Day, but I wouldn’t wait much longer. The good news is that you can get a trip credit if the price drops after you lock in the ticket (as long as you don’t book ‘basic’ economy),” he told Nexstar via email, pointing to airfare tracking tools that allow you to monitor flights and earn trip credits automatically.

If you aren’t ready to book yet, you can also set up Google Flight Alerts to track trip prices. Henderson noted, though, that prices are expected to jump after Labor Day.

He anticipates that for those traveling over the upcoming holidays, “resort destinations will be most expensive,” including both ski sites and tropical locations. That includes Aspen and Vail in Colorado; Big Sky, Montana; Sun Valley, Idaho; and Jackson Hole, Wyoming; as well as Maui, Kauai, and Honolulu in Hawaii.

If you are hoping to save some money on your flight, Henderson said layovers can help, “especially if you’re willing to spend as much as eight hours in an airport.” Other tips include using points or miles, and booking vacation packages that include your flight, hotel and car rental all in one.

As for airfare for non-holiday-travel flights, it doesn’t appear that much relief is on the horizon, either.

Jet fuel is expected to cost 70% more this year on average than in 2025, according to the International Air Transport Association.

“The likelihood that fuel surcharges are going to be rolled back and airfares are going to be brought down is very low over the next few months,” Brett House, a Columbia University economist, told The Associated Press. “There is less choice for consumers and less competition between airlines, and therefore, less pressure to rein in fare increases.”

Sununu, meanwhile, said Sunday that prices could level off.

“I think they’re going to be kind of stabilized for quite a while because we’re not getting out of this Iran thing anytime soon, unfortunately.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Tuesday she probably would not date a conservative, citing the importance of shared values in a relationship.

The New York Democrat laughed when a TMZ reporter approached her on Capitol Hill and asked her whether she would ever consider dating a conservative.

“I have to say it’s, uh, probably not,” she said.

Asked whether she would advise against “dating across the aisle,” Ocasio-Cortez said she had no issue with people who choose to do so, but she suggested differing opinions in politics can reflect broader disagreements over values.

“How you define that is very different from person to person,” she said. “I think a lot of politics sometimes, at least for me, is about values, and being aligned in values I think is tremendously important.”

She reportedly split from her longtime fiance, technology consultant Riley Roberts, two years ago and has been publicly documenting her journey in freezing her eggs . She said the fertility process would give her more time to decide whether she wants to have children while focusing on her political career.

Ocasio-Cortez, who has been poised as a potential contender for the 2028 presidential race, said she found some of the backlash to her fertility journey “funny,” pointing to critiques from commentators after she posted videos to social media documenting the process.

“I also find the freak-out around it pretty funny as well. I’m not going to lie,” the lawmaker said in a 10-minute video documenting the sixth day of her egg-freezing process.

“Some commentator was like, ‘What she’s doing is peddling the dangerous lie that women can have it all,’” she continued. “You know, I find it very funny because the way of life that conservatives are trying to push out there, which is to marry young and have lots of kids at a young age.”

Conservative podcaster Katie Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, defended Ocasio-Cortez’s decision to freeze her eggs, saying that if a woman makes the decision to preserve her ability to have children one day, “we should celebrate that.”

articles.title: Kennedy Center removing landmark sculpture from grounds
articles.summary: The Kennedy Center is set to take down a towering sculpture from the center’s grounds on Wednesday. The artwork’s removal comes amid a wave of changes at the...
articles.body:
The Kennedy Center is set to take down a towering sculpture from the center's grounds on Wednesday.

The artwork's removal comes amid a wave of changes at the renowned Washington performing arts center during President Trump's second term.

The 24-foot aluminum sculpture, named "Blue," was gifted to the center in 2019. The art, which was created by famed American postminimalist sculptor Joel Shapiro, depicts a human stick figure "poised in mid-kick," according to the Kennedy Center's description .

The National Park Service implemented a temporary road closure starting early Wednesday morning to facilitate the removal, according to a public notice .

The sculpture is located along the Video Wall at the REACH, a $250 million addition to the center that opened in 2019. The project is an acronym of renew, experience, activate, create and honor — words meant to encapsulate former President Kennedy's "vision for a new frontier for the arts," the center's website explains.

The center directed the sculpture's removal, and its relocation will be determined by a foundation dedicated to the artist, a spokesperson for the performing arts venue told The Hill.

"We are deeply grateful to Joel Shapiro for the years 'Blue' has spent animating our campus and connecting visitors to his vision," the spokesperson said. "We are honored to have been stewards of his vibrant work and a part of his enduring legacy."

They also noted that gifted or loaned artworks are frequently deinstalled at art institutions across the world.

The removal of "Blue" comes amid a backdrop of tension over the Trump administration's efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center.

The president's push to have his name inscribed on the performing arts center's sign and shut down the venue for restoration projects has resulted in an ongoing legal battle. Ohio Rep. Joyce Beatty (D), an ex officio Kennedy Center board member, has sued to halt the changes.

In federal court on Thursday, the Justice Department defended the administration's efforts to add Trump's name to the building and claimed the iconic arts center was in "structural and financial disarray."

Beatty's lawyer, Nathaniel Zelinsky, accused the center's current board members of engaging in "outright defiance" of the court and argued that the institution was now in "crisis" because of this renaming effort.

articles.title: Anger over planned AI data center drives Missouri city’s voters to recall council member
articles.summary: Voters in Independence, Missouri, voted to recall a city council member over his decision in March to back billions of dollars in tax breaks for an AI data center.
articles.body: Voters in Independence, Missouri, on Tuesday night voted to recall a City Council member who has served for more than a decade, rebuking his decision in March to back billions of dollars in tax breaks for a proposed AI data center. The recall effort comes amid escalating backlash nationwide against the rapid proliferation of data centers that is influencing federal and local races ahead of November’s midterm elections. Independence City Councilmember John Perkins was recalled Tuesday, with nearly 70% of his district voting to remove him, according to unofficial election results from Jackson County. The anger in Independence, a Kansas City suburb with 121,000 residents, over the construction of the artificial intelligence data center on the city’s eastern flank has been mounting for months. In March, Perkins was one of five council members who voted to issue tax breaks totaling more than $6 billion to Dutch company Nebius for the construction of the planned $150 billion data center. More than 50 community members attended and spoke at the City Council meeting in which the tax breaks were approved. A local chapter of the progressive Sunrise Movement organized a letter-writing campaign ahead of the meeting for community members to oppose the tax breaks in an attempt to sink the data center project. A Facebook group for Independence residents who oppose the data center called Stop the AI Data Center in Independence has 115,000 members, many who celebrated Tuesday night when the unofficial election results showed Perkins had been recalled. “Politicians aren’t entitled to elected positions. They’re elected by the people to serve those people. When they stop serving the people they were elected to represent, they’re voted out of office,” one member of the group wrote Tuesday. “This is democracy in action.” Another member of the group described speaking with Perkins outside their polling place Tuesday, writing that they’d told him, “Enjoy the consequences of selling us out to the data center.” Perkins has not yet responded to a request for comment on the recall election. But in a recent Kansas City Star op-ed, he urged voters to judge him by his full record, adding that he stood by the data center vote. “You can disagree with that call, and I respect that,” Perkins wrote. “However, disagreement isn’t a crime, and I don’t believe it is grounds to attempt to overturn an election that happened two years ago.” Two other City Council members who’d voted in favor of the data center tax breaks — Bridget McCandless and Jared Fears — lost their subsequent election bids in April. Fears was running for re-election to the council and McCandless was running for mayor. Opposition to AI data centers has surfaced in communities around the country, looming over the coming midterms and prompting candidates to choose sides. For some Republicans, that has meant opposing President Donald Trump, who recently signaled strong support for data centers — writing on Truth Social that communities that oppose them “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

articles.title: Trumpisms are the Republicans’ biggest messaging problem
articles.summary: If you actually want to win an election which is a referendum on Trump’s presidency, I suggest you get the president off camera and take his phone away.
articles.body:
As we approach the 2026 midterms, one thing is absolutely clear. Republicans are in serious trouble. With each passing week, their prospects worsen. The one constant in this worsening picture is President Trump’s dominance of the Republican messaging machine.

I know my MAGA diehard friends are going to say that Trump is the best messenger ever. That is true — if you are willing to settle for 33 percent of the electorate . If you actually want to win an election that is a referendum on Trump’s presidency, I suggest you get him off camera and take his phone away.

Trump’s incessant comments about issues voters do not care about is an anchor around the neck of Republicans running in anything resembling a competitive district or state. Webster’s could define whiplash as an injury inflicted on anyone who attempts to follow Trump’s weekly policy reversals.

For my MAGA friends, it is time to understand that Trump’s gut does not rule the world. As we approach the midpoint of his second term presidency it is more than disconcerting to watch the president idle away news cycles doodling on his plans for a White House ballroom or a redesign of Dulles Airport. The president has reverted to his days as a developer, a profession in which progress is defined as moving dirt.

That is not how hardworking American families define progress. Those families are struggling over a legal pad penciled in dollar signs trying to figure out if they have enough money to take the kids out for pizza on Friday night.

And Trump does what? He threatens Oman, our ally. He launches an economic attack on Canada , hurting local economies in Maine, upstate New York and Michigan. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is up for reelection, and Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) can’t be happy about that. Perhaps someone in the White House will ask Buffalo area businesses how much traffic has decreased crossing the Peace Bridge from Ontario into Buffalo during the Trump second term.

Trump blames Senate Republicans for not passing his sacred SAVE Act while ignoring the plethora of respected surveys indicating that he is leading Republicans to a significant defeat in November.

A compilation of Senate polls shows Republican candidates trailing or tied in Maine, Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Alaska. Iowa is close to joining the list. Consider this: soybeans, fertilizer, tariffs, John Deere. I think you can make some money on FanDuel betting the over on any Democrat running in the farm belt.

It would be helpful if someone in the White House could convince the president that people do not vote on political process issues like repealing the filibuster. Americans vote on issues that affect the economic wellbeing of their family. When voters are focused on finances and their political leadership ignores it, voters will act to change the leadership.

This is what happens when the person in charge always believes that he is the smartest person in the room. Trump has developed a habit of denigrating the fact-based positions of others who disagree with him or offer anything other than praise.

First, President Trump has dismissed affordability issues as a “ hoax ” perpetrated by Democrats and said, “ this is the golden age of America .” He said the USS Lincoln was not deployed long enough in spite of documented supply and morale problems on board. He said Iran no longer had “any spotters,” “anti-aircraft” or “radar” — until they shot down two American jets two days later. He then unilaterally claimed the Strait of Hormuz as “American territory”.

Such utterances from a president evoke President Lyndon Johnson’s 1965 Vietnam credibility gap . In a recent editorial entitled “ Trump’s Iran Credibility Problem ,” The Wall Street Journal called for “more resolve and consistency than Mr. Trump has shown in the past six months.”

Trump’s insistence last year on H.R.1 — the “One, Big, Beautiful Bill” — cost Republicans the opportunity to drive a message such as “The Tax Reduction for Working Families Act.” Trump’s version unfortunately polled negatively when it was being debated and still does.

It was Trump, in a shocking display of petulance, who blew up the signing ceremony for the housing bill, denying embattled congressional Republican the opportunity to stand with him amid a sea of red, white and blue and celebrate accomplishing something American families wanted.

My prescription to help Republicans salvage at least a tie in the Senate in the upcoming midterms is for President Trump to sit down, talk a lot less and stay off camera. You and I both know that is never going to happen — not now, and not in 2028.

As we approach 2028, that will be a problem for Vice President JD Vance. At least now, he will not be surprised by what is to come.

Kevin Igoe is the former deputy chief of staff of the Republican National Committee and former executive director of the Maryland Republican Party. He served as chief of staff of the Maryland Department of Budget and Management and was a Reagan White House appointee.

articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on Wednesday threw her support behind Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist running for U.S. Senate.

In a statement shared on social media , the New York lawmaker said Nixon would be “an exemplary fighter for the working families of Florida.”

“She did not get here by yielding to major political machines, she did it by building community power and fiercely committing to her values,” Ocasio-Cortez continued. “That’s why I’m proud to endorse her for the U.S. Senate.”

Nixon wrote in a social media post that she was “honored” by the lawmaker’s endorsement.

“AOC [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] is a fighter and a reminder of what’s possible when you put the needs of the people first, instead of protecting the interests of the wealthy and well-connected,” she wrote in a follow-up post . “Florida deserves, & is ready for, the kind of leadership in the U.S. Senate that has been absent for far too long.”

In Florida’s Democratic primary last month, Nixon bested Alex Vindman, a star witness during the first Trump impeachment. The win was a major victory for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which has seen a number of its members oust establishment Democrats this primary cycle.

Nixon is up against incumbent GOP Sen. Ashley Moody (Fla.) in the general election this November. The Republican was tapped by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to replace Marco Rubio in the Senate after his nomination to lead the State Department.

Moody, who is endorsed by President Trump, has criticized Nixon for her past support of the Council on American-Islamic Relations and her DSA membership.

“I am up against probably what would be the most extreme, radical senator ever in the history of the United States in Angie Nixon,” Moody told Fox News last month.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates the race as solid Republican. Florida voters have supported Trump in the past three presidential elections.

articles.title: Why America should fear gerrymandering, not voter fraud
articles.summary: For those who claim that their election was stolen, the appropriate response is: “show me the evidence.” As for gerrymandering, the evidence already exists in every state congressional map, in plain sight for all to witness.
articles.body:
The 2026 midterms are fast approaching, and discussions of voter fraud are ubiquitous . Yet election manipulation is certain to occur during the midterms — though much of it will have little to do with how votes are cast or counted.

Rather, it is how congressional maps were redrawn in several states over the past year to ensure that certain candidates would win their seats. In doing so, and by shifting attention away from partisan district boundaries to the voters themselves, politicians have normalized map meddling while guiding voters to look for threats in all the wrong places.

Since 2020, there has been a new standard mode of operation spreading for elected officials; they either win their election, or if they lose, they claim that the election was stolen from them.

Those claiming stolen elections have been from both the Republican and Democratic parties. The phenomenon has become more visible, amplified by social media , dating back to the 2020 election when Joe Biden defeated incumbent President Trump . However, it was heard even in 2016, when then candidate Donald Trump, anticipating a loss to Hillary Clinton, preemptively claimed that the election could be rigged against him. After Trump won, Clinton proceeded to claim that the election was stolen from her .

The issue up for debate is whether election vote counts can be manipulated to yield a different outcome. In theory, they can. However, the more salient issue is whether such manipulation can be executed with no evidence left behind for others to uncover during audits or recounts.

There are numerous ways that states conduct elections and count votes . Multiple layers of infrastructure make a large-scale manipulation of votes without detection very difficult. There has also been no evidence that foreign actors have successfully changed votes or, more importantly, changed the outcome in a U.S. federal election.

For a person or group to compromise the outcome of an election, voting infrastructure or ballots would have to be tampered with so that a vote for one candidate would be disqualified or counted for another candidate. Even with guardrails placed around these infrastructures, including bipartisan review and handling protocols, small-scale irregularities can occur. But it is extraordinarily difficult to covertly alter enough votes to change the election outcome without leaving behind incriminating evidence.

If paper ballots are used or are available, then a paper trail exists to count and, if necessary, recount ballots. Around 99 percent of registered voters live in an area that offers some form of paper vote documentation. Such physical records provide a natural audit trail that helps protect the integrity of the election and the results.

When one begins to stack all these unlikely events together, it becomes clear that accusations of election fraud lack credible evidence.

Yet Trump and many of his political allies have continued along this path. This recently included Mike Lindell, who lost his primary race for governor to Lisa Demuth by 11 points. His claims of irregularities in the vote totals are a continuation of such rhetoric. Note that when election irregularities have been investigated, the outcomes have rarely led to an overturn of the certified election results. There are exceptions, of course; after Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) lost his primary, he explicitly denounced those who claim election fraud.

The U.S. Constitution leaves most election administration to the states . Yet there is another form of election manipulation that the Constitution is silent on: gerrymandering . With computational redistricting algorithms , mapmakers can configure voters into districts, packing some voters together and cracking others apart, producing districts in which the general-election outcomes are insensitive to changes in voter shifts.

Forecasts for the 2026 midterm election show that 21 of the 435 House Seats are toss-ups, and another 16 are leaning to one party , according to the Cook Political Report . Unlike covert vote manipulation, gerrymandering represents electoral manipulation that is overtly measurable and often legal under current laws, with negative consequences for democracy .

Undoubtedly, individual votes can be manipulated. But translating such manipulation into changed election outcomes that remain undetected is very difficult. On the other hand, election manipulation via gerrymandering is openly and unabashedly done by state lawmakers, taking the power of choice away from voters.

The biggest threat to the value of an individual vote may not be someone secretly changing it. It may be drawing a district with such care that the outcome is effectively determined before the voter ever enters the booth.

Ultimately, for those who claim that their election was stolen, the appropriate response is: “Show me the evidence.” As for gerrymandering, the evidence already exists in every state congressional map, in plain sight for all to witness.

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor in computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. As a data scientist, he applies his expertise in data-driven, risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy. He serves as the director of the Institute for Computational Redistricting.

articles.title: US Mint officially launches $1 coin featuring Trump
articles.summary: The United States Mint released 250,000 $1 coins Wednesday featuring President Trump’s likeness to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. The design of the coin shows a simple portrait of the president — designed by United States Mint Chief Engraver Joseph Menna and inspired by an official White House photo by Daniel Torok — on one…
articles.body:
The United States Mint released 250,000 $1 coins Wednesday featuring President Trump’s likeness to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The design of the coin shows a simple portrait of the president — designed by United States Mint Chief Engraver Joseph Menna and inspired by an official White House photo by Daniel Torok — on one side with the inscriptions “Liberty,” “In God We Trust” and “1776 ~ 2026.”

The coin was greenlighted in March after controversy arose stemming from a federal law that previously prohibited living people from being depicted on U.S. currency. But a law Trump signed during his first term — called the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020 — included new language regarding the semiquincentennial commemoration coins.

The Trump administration also told Newsweek it does not need congressional approval for the coin — citing a history of coins with the likeness of the sitting president such as a 150th anniversary coin with former President Calvin Coolidge as one example in a legal filing.

The other side of the new coin has the insignia from the Presidential Seal, which shows an eagle holding an olive branch, a bundle of arrows with a shield on its breast and a banner. This side contains the inscription “250” to honor the semiquincentennial of the U.S.

The coins have a gold-like finish but a nonprecious metal composition. They are being minted in Philadelphia and will be available Sept. 2 in 25-coin rolls and 100-coin bags.

The U.S. Mint noted that the coins were never placed into circulation but “may be still used as legal tender.”

The U.S. Mint is already offering several commemorative coins this year, including “Revolutionary War Quarters,” “American Eagle Gold Coins” and “Enduring Liberty Half Dollars” — with some valued at more than $10,000.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated the coin featuring Trump “celebrates the strength of American values, and the promise of a nation dedicated to preserving freedom for all.”

He has also led the Treasury Department to print new currency with the president’s signature earlier this year.

Other projects by the Trump administration to add the president’s name and likeness have also received criticism — notably in an ongoing legal battle to add Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center.

A new plan would add an inscription reading “Restored and Renovated by President Donald Trump” after a federal judge ruled against an earlier proposal that would alter the center’s official name, finding that only Congress could change the center’s name.
