articles.title: Trump admin backs OpenAI ‘fair use’ argument in suit from New York Times
articles.summary: President Trump’s administration is signaling support of OpenAI as it defends itself from a lawsuit brought by The New York Times over fair use of the outlet’s content. The Times sued OpenAI in 2023 over the use of its journalism to train its systems and popular chatbots, which are used by millions of people across…
articles.body:
President Trump’s administration is signaling support of OpenAI as it defends itself from a lawsuit brought by The New York Times over fair use of the outlet’s content.

The Times sued OpenAI in 2023 over the use of its journalism to train its systems and popular chatbots, which are used by millions of people across the country for work, business and entertainment.

In a new filing this week, the Trump administration signaled support for OpenAI.

Having a “robust” AI ecosystem in the U.S., lawyers for the federal government said in the filing, is essential for national security and other government priorities, and OpenAI should be able to use even copyrighted content to advance its technology.

“It would be problematic—and legally incorrect—to impose broad copyright liability that would generally render training of AI models impermissible without licensing,” the government said.

The Times has argued in court filings and public statements that OpenAI should not be able to publish its journalism, which is based on original reporting, without its consent.

The case is being widely watched as news publishers grapple with the emergence of AI platforms that are feeding a growing number of search engines and social media platforms where consumers look for news and information.

Times leadership has signaled it is open to working with AI platforms but that its copyrighted journalism should be off limits from feeding OpenAI’s chatbots and other systems.

“Tech giants strip-mine news websites without permission or compensation. They repackage these stolen goods as their own, siphoning off the audiences and revenue that otherwise would go to the news organizations that created this work. And this happens not just once during the training process, but countless times every single day,” Times publisher A.G. Sulzberger said during a speech this summer at the World News Media Congress.

“News organizations should want the good A.I. can bring. But tech companies should also want to support the healthy, sustainable flow of the information and ideas and creativity that powers A.I. — to ensure their actions don’t lead us to a tragedy of the civic commons.”

OpenAI has so far unsuccessfully attempted to convince a judge to toss the Times’s case, while the newspaper has struck partnerships with other AI providers like Amazon.

“I remain convinced of the value created by quality news organizations dedicated to the hard, expensive work of original reporting — to readers, to communities, to society as a whole. And, yes, even to A.I. models,” Sulzberger said. “The question is whether that value will be leached up by tech giants, or whether that value will return to news organizations to allow them to continue this essential work.”

articles.title: Tiger Woods pleads no contest to reckless driving charge, gets license suspended for 5 years
articles.summary: Woods told officers at the scene the crash occurred while he was looking at his phone and changing the radio.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) – Tiger Woods attended a hearing on Wednesday morning to plead no-contest to a reckless driving charge stemming from a rollover crash in Florida earlier this year. The deal stipulates Woods will have his license suspended for five years and pay $1,500 in fines.

Woods initially pleaded not guilty to careless driving and DUI damage to property or persons.

On March 27, Woods’ Land Rover struck a White Ford, causing the Rover to lose control and flip on the driver’s side, according to an incident report from the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The truck was making a right turn when Woods moved into the oncoming traffic lane, striking the vehicle.

Woods told officers at the scene the crash had occurred while he was looking at his phone and changing the radio, and he did not notice the vehicle in front of him slow down. The crash caused $5,000 in damage to the truck, according to the report.

Woods exited the vehicle by climbing out the passenger side. Neither driver sustained injuries from the crash. Woods was reported to be exhibiting several signs of impairment , including slow movements and glassy eyes, and was sweating profusely. Officers noted he was very alert during the investigation.

Woods agreed to a breathalyzer test, which showed no signs of alcohol, but refused a urine test. Officers discovered two hydrocodone pills in his pocket. Woods told officers he’d taken prescription medication and denied taking illegal substances.

articles.title: Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz after himself
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday floated changing the name of the Strait of Hormuz to the Trump Strait, despite the waterway not having a single owner. “Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump wrote…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday floated changing the name of the Strait of Hormuz to the Trump Strait, despite the waterway not having a single owner.

“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The strait is an international waterway that has some water in Oman and Iran territories.

The idea of naming the body of water after the president comes after Trump has also suggested that he will make the strait a U.S. territory.

“Pretty soon, I will be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said during remarks last month.

He has not elaborated on how he would change the strait’s name or make the critical shipping lane a U.S. territory.

Roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas is shipped through the waterway. The war with Iran has slowed traffic, sending energy prices skyrocketing worldwide. The U.S. maintains its naval blockade on the shipping route.

The war with Iran has surpassed the six-month mark, and still no deals have been made to end the fighting or end Iran’s nuclear program.

The U.S. launched a new wave of strikes on Tehran on Tuesday. Trump has said he is “not trying to force Iran to the negotiating table.”

“I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Trump stated Tuesday on Truth Social . “They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”

articles.title: House Republican on Trump ground beef import plan: ‘Damage is done’
articles.summary: Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) responded Tuesday to President Trump’s plan to pause tariffs on beef imports, saying “the damage is done.” In an interview on NewsNation, host Leland Vittert asked Downing if GOP lawmakers are pressuring the president to reverse the decision. “That’s already affected the market,” Downing said. “So really what we need to…
articles.body:
Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) responded Tuesday to President Trump’s plan to pause tariffs on beef imports, saying “the damage is done.”

In an interview on NewsNation, host Leland Vittert asked Downing if GOP lawmakers are pressuring the president to reverse the decision.

“That’s already affected the market,” Downing said. “So really what we need to do is have, you know, serious conversations with the administration before making decisions like this.”

“I understand his motivations — but before doing this, make sure you’re talking to the stakeholders. Make sure you’re talking to us to understand what the unintended consequences are, especially on timing,” he continued.

The response concerns a plan by Trump to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs, a move intended to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices. The exemption arrives while the president has simultaneously threatened Canada with 50 percent tariffs on its goods.

Trump defended the 90-day suspension in an August Truth Social post , saying, “We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices. This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”

The president notably did not say where the beef would be coming from.

Senate Republicans have already publicly criticized the exemptions, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) calling it a “mistake.”

“If you think that providing subsidized beef for some period of time is going to make farmers happy and prices go down on a systemic basis, you’re wrong. It doesn’t happen,” Tillis said.

Tillis and Downing are two of several Republican lawmakers from agriculture-heavy states to warn against allowing cheap beef imports to flood the U.S. market over the next three months.

Downing added in his appearance that in Montana, “we’ve got about twice as many cows as people.”

“Our ranchers are producing the best beef in the world. … They need to have market stability,” Downing said. “You know, don’t move a market as my producers are going to market, and that’s our biggest issue there.”

Beef prices have been soaring across the country, with the average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound in the U.S. at roughly $6.89 — according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis .

Despite demand for the staple remaining high, Downing says, “We are at an all-time low or a historic low in the herd size.”

He cited “a number of reasons,” which can include droughts and lack of grazing lands — experts also include rising operational costs.

articles.title: Fox News host says Trump made her husband Transportation secretary ‘because that was all that’s left’
articles.summary: Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy on Tuesday said President Trump tapped her husband, Sean Duffy, to be Transportation secretary “because that was all that’s left.” The two were interviewed on “The Katie Miller Podcast,” hosted by the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. The host asked about their conversation after Trump…
articles.body:
Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy on Tuesday said President Trump tapped her husband, Sean Duffy, to be Transportation secretary “because that was all that’s left.”

The two were interviewed on “ The Katie Miller Podcast ,” hosted by the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. The host asked about their conversation after Trump nominated Duffy.

“He said he wanted to serve the president in any way,” Campos-Duffy said. “He ended up in Transportation because that was all that’s left.”

Duffy, himself a former Fox News host, interjected and said he believed Trump when he told him, “If I wasn’t the president, I would pick the Department of Transportation over any department. It’s the best department, and I’m going to give it to you.”

The secretary then emphasized Trump’s focus on construction, having been a developer for much of his life, and said the U.S. has “a president who cares about the infrastructure of America. Usually, presidents don’t give a darn.”

Campos-Miller later said that given her closeness to the administration through her husband and role at Fox News, she does not “talk about anything to do with transportation, and Fox wouldn’t want me to and I don’t want to.”

“It’s no secret that Rachel Campos-Duffy loves President Donald Trump,” she said, causing Miller to laugh. “I was with him when he came down the escalator [in New York City’s Trump Tower in 2015]. I was very early on and even in the dark years when he was out of office and a lot of people had a lot of beef with him and he was facing all the criminal charges .”

Duffy, who also served as NASA’s acting administrator in 2025, and Campos-Duffy have been married since 1999.

The two host a reality series titled “The Great American Road Trip,” which prompted the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington to call on the Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General to investigate Duffy’s role in the show and whether he violated any federal regulations or laws in filming the series.

Campos-Duffy defended her husband, saying he’s not a “ corrupt man .”

Duffy previously co-hosted Fox Business Network’s “The Bottom Line” before Trump asked him to join his second administration. Campos-Duffy guest-hosted on Fox News’s “Outnumbered” before she became a permanent co-host of “Fox & Friends Weekend” in 2021.

Trump also hired former “Fox & Friends Weekend” co-host Pete Hegseth to be Defense secretary and former Fox News host Dan Bongino to serve as deputy director of the FBI before he resigned in January.

Trump has long favored Fox News’s coverage of his administrations, though not without some criticism when their coverage refers to his low approval rating or remarks from critics .

articles.title: Justice Department defends Pentagon’s proposed firings of Stars and Stripes staffers
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) is defending the Pentagon’s plan to dismiss three Stars and Stripes staffers for alleged insubordination, pushing back against claims that the decisions were made partially in retaliation for the military outlet’s coverage of conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) is defending the Pentagon’s plan to dismiss three Stars and Stripes staffers for alleged insubordination, pushing back against claims that the decisions were made partially in retaliation for the military outlet’s coverage of conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte sued the Department of Defense (DOD) last Thursday, seeking a court order that would block the department from terminating them.

The staffers have alleged that the Pentagon is attempting to fire them “for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations,” in addition to other First Amendment violations.

The dispute involves comments made by Korte and Slavin during a July interview on “CBS Sunday Morning” regarding the military newspaper’s editorial independence.

Justice Department attorneys argued in a late Tuesday filing that those remarks were not constitutionally protected because they were made within the scope of the staffers’ “official duties as Stripes personnel.”

“Because Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte spoke pursuant to their official duties, their proposed separations do not implicate the First Amendment, whatever the wisdom of the Department’s personnel judgment,” the filing, signed by U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, stated.

The three staffers were issued separation notices on Aug. 21, with officials citing “insubordination and violations of regulations based on their CBS statements” as the grounds for Slavin and Korte’s dismissal, according to court documents.

Lederer’s notice cited his refusal to deliver separation notices to the two other employees, among other reasons, as justification for his termination. The publisher announced his retirement on Aug. 19 amid concerns about the editorial direction of the outlet under the Trump administration.

“Delivering or declining to deliver those notices is the performance or non-performance of a supervisory task, not the speech of a citizen,” DOJ attorneys wrote. “Plaintiffs’ theory that the refusal was protected because Mr. Slavin’s and Ms. Korte’s speech was protected, fails with its premise: to deliver a notice of separation is not speech, regardless of whether the separation is justified.”

The government also objected to arguments that the firings were an attempt to punish the staffers for unfavorable coverage on the Lincoln’s extended deployment, claiming the decision was made weeks before the article was published.

All three were placed on administrative leave, and the Pentagon has agreed to pause their terminations until at least Sept. 4 while legal proceedings continue. A hearing has been scheduled for Friday.

Stars and Stripes has operated independently from the Defense Department since 1993, with internal policies stating it should be free from “news management or censorship,” even though it is partially funded by the Pentagon.

But the Trump administration has sought to reshape the newspaper’s editorial output in recent months, with Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell saying in January that it would “ modernize its operations ” and “refocus its content away from woke distractions.”

The Pentagon is facing additional lawsuits from the paper’s ombudsman and two advisory board members over accusations that the administration is trying to undermine its independence and censor its content.

articles.title: House Democrats face fallout from shock defections
articles.summary: Plus: 🎵 Dollyfest is coming in 2027! {beacon} It’s Wednesday. We have officially entered the late 2020s. Just 1,217 days until the early 2030s. Carpe decennium! In today’s issue: Two Democrats save GOP Navy Secretary nomination Chevron strikes deal with Venezuela Dollyfest in 2027 Programming note: We’re Abigail Walker and Joshua Feldstein, filling…
articles.body:
It’s Wednesday. We have officially entered the late 2020s. Just 1,217 days until the early 2030s. Carpe decennium!

Programming note : We’re Abigail Walker and Joshua Feldstein , filling in for Cate today. Please send me your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) shocked Democratic House leadership on Tuesday when they chose to join Republicans in advancing a GOP-backed rule.

“The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), along with Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), said in a joint statement.

The legislation included a messaging bill condemning socialism, a message integral to the Republican’s midterm strategy.

Some Democrats want heads to roll: The Democratic leaders said the defections necessitate a “serious response” and said they asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order.”

It’s unclear what potential punishment would be, but some Democrats are reportedly pushing for Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez to lose committee assignments.

“We have to draw a bright line here and kick some a– or this will be the new norm,” “I ‘effing love it,” Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios .

This is not normal: Helen Huiskes and Mike Lillis : “Traditionally, the majority party votes in favor of rules, which tee up debate and final votes on bills, while the minority party votes against them, regardless of how lawmakers plan to vote on the underlying legislation.”

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) summed it up succinctly: “We never had that problem,” she told reporters .

“No, no, no,” Rep. Jim McGovern (D) said after the vote. “Who are we, the Republicans?”

Golden response : Golden, who’s leaving Congress, said the GOP-backed rule included a bill, the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act, he proposed to give lobstermen economic protections from the impact of conservation efforts for the North Atlantic right whale.

“When I first got into Congress, lobstermen were terrified at the scale of these proposed new regulations [to protect whales],” Golden said on the Substack “Out of State.” “It was unworkable to the point where there would be hard discussions in communities about which families get to keep fishing and which had to give it up.”

Gluesenkamp Perez told reporters that she “slept like a baby last night,” and is not worried about Democratic discipline following the vote.

“If that’s what they feel they need to do, it’s not going to change how I represent [my district],” she continued.

President Trump in recent weeks has made numerous attempts to prove to Americans that his administration takes seriously the cost-of-living crisis.

On Monday, the Trump administration announced it secured Medicaid drug pricing deals with nine biotech and pharmaceutical companies. Trump is also pressing ahead with a move to lower ground beef prices despite a furious pushback from cattle ranchers and their allies in Congress. And he framed a major Venezuelan oil agreement as lowering costs at the pump — though it’s going to take a while.

In case anyone missed the message, a pro-Trump political group is out with a new ad highlighting his efforts to cut taxes and fight inflation.

The group, Securing American Greatness, has booked almost $1 million, with ads starting to air on Thursday.

Too little too late? The actions come amid the president’s increasingly poor approval rating. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll had the president’s approval rating hit 33 percent, a 14-point slide from the start of his second term and a 4-point slide from about a month ago.

Trump had long complained that “affordability” was invented by Democrats as an attack line, arguing the Biden administration was to blame for inflation.

Now that he’s tackling the issue head on, The Hill’s Julia Manchester asked GOP strategists if it was too late to change voter attitudes.

“Ads are really just going up on air,” on Republican operative said. “The real spending starts now, post Labor Day, and we’re going to see a ton of resources pour into these districts, and a lot is going to change over the next couple of weeks.”

Hegseth’s overhaul continues : Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday removed at least six Army officers from a list of suggested promotion to two-star generals, a person familiar with the matter told The Hill.

The decision is the most recent in a series of moves Hegseth has made to reshape the military and its leadership.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll , who had a contentious relationship with the Defense secretary, submitted his resignation late last week. On Friday, Hegseth blocked the promotion of four Army officials.

Both Democrats and Republicans have raised their eyebrows at Hegseth’s decision-making.

Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.), a senior Republican on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he was “disappointed” to learn of the Driscoll’s departure. And he said Hegseth would have to answer for his other moves when the Senate returns.

“I’m hearing the same rumors everybody else is that he was frustrated with some of his top generals being released. That’s not the first time I’ve heard that. I think that points to questions that we’re going to be asking when we get back,” Rounds said.

“I’m tired of all the churn,” Rep. Mike Rogers , R-Ala., the chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, told reporters on Tuesday, according to MS NOW . “I want to see some stability over there.”

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell on Friday told The Hill that “Military promotions are given to those who have earned them. This has always been the case under Secretary Hegseth and will not change.”

NAVY NOMINATION: President Trump has nominated acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao for the permanent role, after John Phelan stepped down from the role in April — amid friction with Hegseth.

“We need Patriots like Hung leading our Navy and Marine Corps, and I can think of no one better than him to make sure our Great Navy and Marine Corps remain the FIERCEST and BEST Force the World has ever seen,” Trump said on Truth Social .

“It’s an honor of a lifetime to lead the great warriors of the Navy and Marine Corps,” Cao said in his own post. “I’m grateful for you [Trump] leadership and support as we continue to get after shipbuilding and ensure the defense of the homeland.”

Phelan, a millionaire Trump donor, had served in the role for a little over a year before being “asked to step down,” The Hill’s Filip Timotija reported at the time.

Chevron announced an agreement with Venezuela Wednesday morning, which aims to double the current oil production in the South American country.

The company said that oil production in Venezuela will go up to 600,000 barrels per day, and that the effort will be done through a joint venture, according to The Hill’s Rachel Frazin.

“Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investment within our portfolio for decades,” Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said in a statement.

That follows another major oil deal : President Trump announced last week that the U.S. would have control over a large swath of Venezuela’s oil reserves, securing more than 65 billion barrels.

According to a press release, the Trump administration said that the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital would take 35 percent equity stake in North American Blue Energy Partners , Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer.

North American Blue Energy Partners will now be partially owned by the U.S. and was given a 100-year concession for Venezuelan oil fields.

Trump has encouraged U.S. oil companies to operate in Venezuela. Chevron is currently the only major American oil company that still has operations there.

Iran launched missiles and drones across the Middle East Wednesday morning, targeting U.S. assets in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan and Kuwait, in a retaliatory move following expanded U.S. strikes on Tuesday.

The U.S.’s Tuesday attacks were a response to the Islamic Republic’s strikes on military bases in Jordan earlier this week, according to U.S. Central Command (Centcom). The U.S. started the tit for tat with preemptive strikes on Iranian missile launchers near the Strait of Hormuz.

Assessing the damage : Iran says the wave of U.S. strikes Tuesday night did significant damage to targets along the coast.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) also released a statement that a U.S. airstrike also hit a wedding ceremony at a residential home, killing at least four people and injuring dozens.

What next? President Trump warned Iran before Tuesday’s strikes that any response by Iran would lead to them being “hit again at a much harder and higher level.”

On Tuesday, the president also questioned when the Iranian people “would rise up and fight.”

“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table, as ABC Fake News reported,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “I couldn’t care less if they signed a worthless, to them, agreement.”

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey (D) will face off against Republican challenger Mike Minogue in November’s gubernatorial election. Minogue defeated Brian Shortleeve by over 30 percentage points in Tuesday’s GOP primary.

Former Biden official Daniel Koh (D-Mass.) won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts’s 6th Congressional District, the seat left open by Rep. Seth Moulton (D). He defeated progressive State Rep. Tram Nguyen (D).

The Dallas Police Department announced it is shutting down more than 300 Flock cameras following Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R-Texas) funding halt for the roadside camera network.

Tiger Woods reversed his plea in connection with his latest DUI arrest, agreeing Wednesday to plead no contest to a reckless driving charge and not submitting a sobriety test. The golf legend was arrested in March after he hit a pickup truck and flipped his car in Florida.

Associated Press : US extends ban on flights to Haiti’s capital

Politico : Von der Leyen, Rutte say Russian ‘intimidation will not work’ to stop Ukraine aid

NBC News : Congo Ebola outbreak: Deaths top 3,000 as virus spreads at unprecedented speed

The New York Times : A.I. Is to Be Banned in N.Y.C. Elementary and Middle Schools

The House is in, and the Senate is out. President Trump is in Washington (All times EDT)

A House Judiciary Committee panel on Wednesday will examine the Supreme Court’s recent decision on birthright citizenship and potential legislative responses to it.

A majority of the justices ruled in June to uphold the 14th Amendment practice, citing the Constitution as clearly enshrining jus soli, Latin for “right of the soil.” Following the decision, President Trump signed fresh executive orders targeting birthright citizenship and “birth tourism.”

articles.title: Trump to host group of vulnerable GOP lawmakers at White House
articles.summary: President Trump will host a group of Republican lawmakers facing rough reelection bids for a Rose Garden dinner on Wednesday, the White House confirmed to The Hill. The development comes as lawmakers and candidates approach the post-Labor Day sprint ahead of November’s midterm elections, with many Republicans calling on the president to use his resources…
articles.body:
President Trump will host a group of Republican lawmakers facing rough reelection bids for a Rose Garden dinner on Wednesday, the White House confirmed to The Hill.

The development comes as lawmakers and candidates approach the post-Labor Day sprint ahead of November’s midterm elections, with many Republicans calling on the president to use his resources to boost them in their races.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) is slated to attend, while a source familiar told NewsNation that Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who is facing an uphill Senate bid against incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), will also attend.

Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.) will attend the dinner, according to Politico.

Some Republicans have voiced frustrations that Trump is not spending enough of his money to defend the party’s narrow majority in Congress. However, Trump has signaled that he will spend more ahead of the midterms.

MAGA Inc. spent more than $827,000 to support Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in her primary runoff last month.

“Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump told reporters ahead of a campaign rally for Graham last month. “I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money — but I’ll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates.”

MAGA Inc. is slated to hold two $1 million-per-person fundraisers this fall at Trump National Golf Club in Virginia and at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, according to invitations obtained by CBS News on Monday.

articles.title: House GOP campaign arm distributes more than 2,000 tickets for midterm convention in Texas
articles.summary: The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) distributed more than 2,000 tickets for next week’s midterm convention in Texas, a source familiar with the event told The Hill on Wednesday. The NRCC said around 100 members and candidates were confirmed, though Politico reported on Wednesday that 45 out of 70 Republican candidates and members who were…
articles.body:
The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) distributed more than 2,000 tickets for next week’s midterm convention in Texas, a source familiar with the event told The Hill on Wednesday.

The NRCC said around 100 members and candidates were confirmed, though Politico reported on Wednesday that 45 out of 70 Republican candidates and members who were asked said they were not attending the gathering or were still considering whether they would go.

Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) told Politico that the suggested minimum attendee donation to attend the convention was $25,000.

The source familiar noted the $25,000 suggested donation is cheaper than past conventions.

About 20,000 people are expected to attend, according to John Hiller, White House aide and the CEO of the convention’s organizing board.

The gathering is meant to galvanize the Republican base ahead of the midterms as the party faces historical headwinds and low approval ratings for President Trump.

Trump will appear for both nights of the gathering on Sept. 9 and 10 and deliver remarks on the final night. Vice President Vance will address attendees on the first night of the convention.

According to guidance released by the Republican National Committee, both nights of the convention will feature a total of 109 items and speakers.

articles.title: Platner's replacement faces new Senate campaign headache tied to his son's lobbying
articles.summary: Former State Senator Troy Jackson backed millions in public funds for Maine Maritime Academy while his son was a registered lobbyist for the school.
articles.body: Former state Senator Troy Jackson, who has replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine, backed bills seeking to send millions of dollars in public funds to a college while his son lobbied on its behalf, documents show. Jackson’s son, Chace, was registered as a lobbyist for the Maine Maritime Academy at the same time as his father was serving as president of the Maine Senate, according to state lobbying records. In 2024, the elder Jackson co-sponsored legislation that would have sent $13.4 million to the maritime academy after pushing a bill providing the institution with an additional $2 million per year in 2023, with both pieces of legislation being drafted while Jackson's son was lobbying for the college. "Troy Jackson authored Augusta’s failed status quo and has turned public office into a family affair of self-enrichment," National Republican Senatorial Committee press secretary Bernadette Breslin told Fox News Digital. "He’ll always prioritize personal kickbacks over the needs of working Mainers." 5 THINGS TO KNOW ABOUT GRAHAM PLATNER ALLY POISED TO TAKE ON SUSAN COLLINS Before his son was lobbying on its behalf, Jackson also supported legislation in early 2022 that provided the academy with a one-time $6.8 million payment to fund repairs to one of its buildings. Jackson’s son first registered as a lobbyist for the Maine Maritime Academy in December 2022, according to public records. He renewed his lobbying registration in January 2024, just as his father was co-sponsoring legislation that would have sent over $10 million to the academy. While the Maine Maritime Academy funding boost Jackson backed in 2023 went into effect, his 2024 bill passed the Maine Senate but was never signed into law. "Troy Jackson has fought for working Mainers, and [is] guided by one goal: fixing our broken system so Maine's working families stop getting squeezed while the rich get richer," a spokesperson for the Jackson campaign told the Washington Free Beacon, which first reported on the lobbying records. LIKELY PLATNER REPLACEMENT'S RESURFACED POSTS ON 'DEMOCRACY' COME BACK TO BITE HIM: 'HYPOCRITICAL SOCIALIST' In April, Jackson justified his failed run for governor by claiming that the "status quo isn't working" in Maine because of "special interests, high-priced lobbyists and corporate greed." In addition to representing the Maine Maritime Academy, Chace Jackson works as one of the expensive lobbyists his father has criticized, at one point representing the multinational alcohol company behind premium beverages such as Johnnie Walker whiskey and Don Julio tequila. In 2024, while his father was the Maine Senate president, the younger Jackson represented nine clients. That sum dropped to five clients after his father left the chamber in 2025. AFTER PLATNER IMPLOSION, MAINE DEMOCRATS RUSH TOWARD NEW SENATE NOMINEE DESPITE FRESH WARNING SIGNS A bill targeting an oil and gas giant died in the Maine Senate during Jackson's Maine Senate tenure and while his son was lobbying on behalf of the fossil fuel corporation in question. The former state senator is facing off against incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins in November. Jackson replaced Platner as the Democrat on the ballot after his campaign was hit with a series of controversies, ranging from crude deleted Reddit posts to a Nazi-linked tattoo, which culminated in an allegation of rape, prompting the self-identified oyster farmer to drop out of the race. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Jackson, his son and the Maine Maritime Academy did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

articles.title: Alabama AG Marshall fires back at USPS mail-ballot order critics: ‘This is about securing elections’
articles.summary: Steve Marshall says Democratic AGs are blocking voter roll audits to obstruct Trump's election integrity executive order ahead of the midterms.
articles.body: Republican Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall argues that his Democratic counterparts do not care about election integrity in the same way Republicans do, as they attempt to block measures designed to root out illegal voters they have long claimed do not exist. Marshall addressed a legal challenge brought by 25 Democratic state attorneys general challenging President Donald Trump's executive order that included provisions for federal agencies to help states ensure only citizens receive mail-in ballots, and for the U.S. Postal Service to institute practices to make the ballots trackable. "The left, because they’re concerned about losing at the midterms, want to be able to obstruct this administration’s efforts to ensure the integrity of our elections," Marshall told Fox News Digital this week, ahead of Thursday's oral arguments before U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston. "You have to wonder – when those that are objecting to this – how confident they can be in the security of their elections, as opposed to becoming just a partisan opportunity to ensure the Democrats win and keep conservative voices from being heard, not only in local and state levels of government, but particularly in Washington." DHS PLANS COSTLY CRACKDOWN ON STATES THAT DON’T COOPERATE ON ELECTION SECURITY Marshall led a letter in July from 13 Republican attorneys general, backing the U.S. Postal Service's following up on Trump's March 31 executive order that set up an audit of states' voter rolls. "There shouldn't be a reason why we object to that, but yet Democrats simply don't want to have fair elections in a way that people can have confidence," Marshall claimed. Fox News Digital reached out to the Democratic Attorneys General Association for comment on Marshall's remarks, but they did not immediately respond. Democrats, in various arguments to block the audit of voter rolls before the mailing out of absentee ballots, claim that it would lead to "disenfranchisement," "chaos," "unconstitutional overreach" and a partisan "power grab." Democrats' concern is that if they refuse to share their voter rolls with the Department of Homeland Security and Social Security Administration to crosscheck the eligibility of legal voters, the USPS can stop the mailing of state's absentee ballots. "USPS's interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote," Talwani, appointed by former President Barack Obama, wrote in her restraining order against the Trump administration. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "The postal service is not a partisan organization. As the postmaster said, I think most recently, we're just there to deliver the mail. They're experts in how it is that this can be configured." Marshall stated that the problem of voter fraud is documented, not "unsubstantiated," as Talwani put it, with evidence in his own state. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE "This is not a solution looking for a problem," he said. "This is in response to what we know is going on across the country. And this provides a commonsense, straightforward way for states to be able to ensure elections, but most importantly, for the people of this country to have belief that their elections in fact are accurate." MAIL-VOTING CRACKDOWN MOVES AHEAD AS TRUMP COURT WIN OPENS DOOR TO FEDERAL ACTION "It's not a shock that Democrats are standing up the ability for us to pass the SAVE [America] Act because they don't want to allow for there to be assurances of what is already in the law: That somebody here illegally cannot be able to vote," he added. "But here we have the president being able to make sure that we are allowing for government resources to be used in an appropriate way to simply allow those who are qualified to vote, vote, and those who aren't, don't." Marshall has little confidence that the Obama-appointed judge in Boston is going to side with the Trump administration and the law. "I would be remiss if I didn't say that I would fully expect her to continue with the Democratic Party line," he said. "The Trump administration has already filed a request with the First Circuit to try to get a stay of that order, but yet we're going to continue to battle this case along with the administration and look forward to standing beside them when they obtain this victory." TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS Marshall maintains Republicans are not stopping anyone from getting an absentee ballot – they're just trying to make sure the process is conducted legally and securely. "Here we have a barcode that allows us to be able to connect it directly with the voter – we have the assurance that that ballot is being cast by the person in fact that receives that ballot," he said. "Democrats and Republicans alike ought to praise this as a commonsense effort to be able to restore election integrity in this area, but it's not a shock that Democrats have opposed it." MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES Marhall pointed to the 2005 bipartisan commission chaired by former President Jimmy Carter and former Secretary of State James Baker that identified mailed absentee ballots as being susceptible to fraud. "This is about securing elections, not interfering with states' abilities to conduct elections, and we think that we'll be able to eliminate many of the issues that we've seen, including in Alabama, that have occurred in the past." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The restraining order Talwani issued will remain in place for up to one more week while she considers whether to issue a longer-term preliminary injunction blocking the rule. The hearing is Thursday in Boston, but the fight will go on from states on both sides as the midterm mail-in ballot season officially gets underway.

articles.title: Social media erupts after DeSantis gives ‘Soros’ protester a piece of his mind: ‘Ain’t my first rodeo’
articles.summary: Ron DeSantis fired back at a heckler he accused of being paid by George Soros during a Florida GOP event, telling her "this ain't my first rodeo."
articles.body: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis set social media aflame Tuesday night after he did not hold back in his response to a disruption by a woman he accused of being paid by George Soros, yelling back at her that "this ain’t my first rodeo." DeSantis was touting Florida’s economy at a state GOP campaign event in Tampa when he was interrupted mid-sentence by a heckler. The governor did not hesitate in his response. "Hey, Soros isn't paying you enough because you're not very good at this," he said, pointing to the woman as security personnel approached her in the crowd. "You should try again," DeSantis continued as the crowd booed the heckler. Keeping with the Soros line, DeSantis piled on, "He needs to pay some better talent instead of having people like you show up. This ain't my first rodeo, lady. I've seen it all, and you ain't very good at it." BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER’S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY' After another heckler interrupted the event again that same evening, DeSantis shot back, "Let me just give you guys some advice: standing up and screaming is not effective. Okay?" "I've seen people try to do this over the years," he continued. "Some are more effective than others." "I remember I had Antifa charge me, and one of our FDLE [Florida Department of Law Enforcement] leveled them, and it was funny, and it was good." "But here's the deal," he leaned in. "I think Soros is tightening his wallet because the people he's paying are terrible at this." SOROS PROSECUTOR IN DANGER OF BEING REMOVED AFTER GRIEVING MOM’S DESPERATE ALARM: ‘CAN’T BELIEVE THIS’ "He used to hire people who were really good. Now they're just screeching, and it's almost like, I don't even know what it is. And so, listen, you should be respectful, you should listen. This is part of the civic process," he said. "But, if you're not going to do that, do a better job at protesting, please. Gosh." "THAT'S MY GOVERNOR!!" reacted conservative commentator Eric Daugherty on X, writing, "DeSantis just PUMMELED a leftist heckler who disrupted his speech tonight." Another popular conservative influencer who simply goes by the name Greg reacted, "Soros protester is re-thinking opening her mouth at the RPOF [Republican Party of Florida] Event. DeSantis with the takedown." Another X account, DeSantis Appreciation Society, wrote, "The Tribal Chief @RonDeSantis just bodied a Soros protester into next week at the RPOF event." "DeSantis is a legend. Absolutely obliterated a liberal heckler, lol. Best governor ever!" wrote another popular conservative account going by the name "American Nightmare." ANTIFA-LINKED SITES GO DARK AFTER STATE DEPARTMENT TERROR DESIGNATION OF TECH COLLECTIVE SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In response, a spokesperson for the Soros family’s philanthropic group, the Open Society Foundations, directed Fox News Digital to a 2025 statement that said, "We do not pay people to protest or directly train or coordinate protestors." While the statement called nonviolent public protests "hallmarks of any vibrant society," the group said that "All Open Society grantees are required to comply with the law and we expect our grantees to uphold our shared commitment to human rights, dignity, and nonviolence." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under the Florida Constitution, DeSantis, who is serving his second consecutive term, is not eligible to seek another consecutive term as governor this year. During Tuesday's event, he endorsed a statewide slate of Republicans, including GOP gubernatorial nominee U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds. The event showcased Donalds as well as other Republican candidates, Attorney General James Uthmeier, Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson.

articles.title: Democrats huddle to weigh changes to party rules following surprise defections
articles.summary: House Democrats huddled Wednesday morning to weigh potential changes to internal party rules after a pair of centrist lawmakers crossed the aisle a day earlier to help Republican leaders advance a series of GOP messaging bills that were on track to fail. The defections by Democratic Reps. Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.)…
articles.body:
House Democrats huddled Wednesday morning to weigh potential changes to internal party rules after a pair of centrist lawmakers crossed the aisle a day earlier to help Republican leaders advance a series of GOP messaging bills that were on track to fail.

The defections by Democratic Reps. Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) caught the Democrats off guard and infuriated both party leaders and many members of the caucus.

The episode prompted a special meeting of the Democrats’ Committee on Caucus Rules, which has been charged by leadership with examining possible changes to the party’s internal guidelines in an effort to ensure that Democrats stick together on future rules votes.

Leaving the meeting, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said no decisions have been made, but all options remain on the table.

“It’ll be an ongoing discussion through the vehicles that have been set up, including meetings related to the Committee on Caucus Rules, as well as more informal discussions that will continue to proceed during the balance of the time that we’re here,” Jeffries said.

Asked if the changes, if adopted, would take effect this Congress or the next, he was noncommittal.

“We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out,” he said.

The uproar stems from Tuesday’s vote on a GOP rule governing a series of bills that Republicans sought to pass this week as an 11th-hour flourish lending them momentum and talking points heading into November’s mid-term elections. The legislation included proposals to condemn socialism, roll back environmental protections and bar U.S. universities from participating in boycotts of Israel — all hot-button issues Republicans see as beneficial on the campaign trail.

The rule was poised to fail, because a handful of conservative Republicans voted against it to protest the decision by GOP leaders to fast-track a massive government funding bill earlier in the day. But Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez voted in favor of the rule to put it over the top, rescuing GOP leaders and salvaging much of the Republicans’ remaining pre-election agenda.

Traditionally, the minority party votes uniformly against rules even if individual lawmakers go on to support the underlying legislation on a final vote.

Both lawmakers defended their decisions, saying their yes votes were the only way to ensure that one of the underlying bills — legislation designed to help Atlantic lobstermen retain their jobs — made it to the floor for a final vote.

But many Democrats were furious, not least because neither defector warned leadership of their intention to cross the aisle. Jeffries and his top two deputies, Reps. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), issued a joint statement Tuesday evening calling the defections “a significant breach of trust” — one that demands “a significant response.”

Jeffries said he will be meeting with Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez later in the day on Wednesday.

Some Democrats were sympathetic to the centrists’ decision, noting that Gluesenkamp Perez hails from a conservative-leaning district where a vote for the lobstermen bill could pay dividends at the polls.

Most Democrats, however, argued the importance of keeping the caucus together on rule votes, even if individual lawmakers break away later to support the underlying bills based on regional concerns.

“Procedurally, this is about making sure that we maintain unity, whether we’re in the minority, or when we’re in the majority,” said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), a member of the Committee on Caucus Rules. “Members — all members — have a right to vote their district. And the underlying bill is the opportunity to do that.”

“It’s long understood what the dynamics are related to procedural votes connected to a rule,” Jeffries said.

articles.title: Pro-Trump group releases first general election midterm ad
articles.summary: Securing American Greatness, the nonprofit arm of President Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc., rolled out its first general election ads on Wednesday, featuring Trump front and center. The ads are a part of a national ad buy. According to the political intelligence firm AdImpact, the group booked $995,000 starting on Wednesday. While one of the…
articles.body:
Securing American Greatness, the nonprofit arm of President Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc., rolled out its first general election ads on Wednesday, featuring Trump front and center.

The ads are a part of a national ad buy. According to the political intelligence firm AdImpact, the group booked $995,000 starting on Wednesday.

While one of the ads mentions the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed by Congress, the ads are largely focused on Trump and his agenda.

One ad features Trump ally and UFC President Dana White praising Trump before playing portions of his State of the Union address from earlier this year. The 30-second spot is overlaid with various videos of Trump.

Another 30-second ad features Trump touting the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including provisions like no taxes on tips, overtime and social security. Trump is also heard in the spot touting the decrease in the price of eggs, his administration’s policies to lower prescription drug prices and telling major companies to pay for their own power needs.

“He’s fighting for you every day. Help him finish the job,” the narrator says.

The ads come as some Republicans have voiced frustrations that Trump is not spending enough of his money to defend the party’s narrow majority in Congress. However, Trump has signaled that he will spend more ahead of the midterms.

MAGA Inc spent more than $827,000 to support Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in her primary runoff last month.

“Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump told reporters ahead of a campaign rally for Graham last month. “I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money — but I’ll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates.”

articles.title: A year into Trump’s boat strike campaign, families search for answers
articles.summary: While the Trump administration claims it has killed ‘narcoterrorists’, families fear fishermen are among the victims.
articles.body:
Rayshawn Charlery stands on a dock in Saint Lucia, his heavy-lidded eyes looking out at the colourful Caribbean fishing boats dotting the bay. He last saw his father, fisherman Joseph “Nathy” William, a week before his disappearance in February.

On February 13, William went fishing with Ricky Joseph, a father of four. Neither returned home. Charlery could no longer reach his father.

That same day, the United States military released black-and-white drone footage of a strike on a small vessel in the Caribbean Sea, saying it had killed suspected narcotics traffickers.

Charlery has doubts about that account. He fears the slender boat may have been a fishing vessel – namely, the one his father was using the day he went missing. His father, he says, was not a drug smuggler.

“All I know is that my father is a fisherman, and he went out to sea and never made it home,” Charlery told the Al Jazeera programme Fault Lines . “He’s just an honest fisherman.”

Charlery’s father left behind two children and an elderly mother he had been caring for.

Since September 2, 2025, the administration of President Donald Trump has carried out dozens of bombings against unidentified vessels in the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific, killing more than 220 people it labels as “narcoterrorists”.

In each case, there has been no court filing, no trial and no public effort to identify the victims. For families like Charlery’s, there have only been images of smoke, silence and the sea.

Experts say the strikes likely amount to extrajudicial killings, which are illegal under international law.

Fault Lines investigated the cases of three missing fishermen and spoke to the families they left behind to offer a window into the human cost of a campaign carried out with little transparency or accountability.

Other families that Fault Lines approached would not speak publicly, for fear of repercussions.

Like Charlery, Ricky Joseph’s family also tried to contact him but could not reach him. Other fishermen sent Titus Joseph, his brother, videos of boat wreckage circulating online. Titus instinctively knew whose vessel it was.

“I said that’s my little brother that was captaining the boat,” Titus told Fault Lines , calling Joseph his “backbone”.

Ricky often supported his family with the few thousand dollars he earned from fishing each year, according to his partner Lucillia Charles. He was the sole breadwinner, providing for her and the children.

Neither Charlery nor Charles was able to get answers from local authorities or the US government about what happened to their loved ones. Both say they went to the police to file a missing persons report. They did not hear back.

Fault Lines asked local police in Saint Lucia for answers about both cases, but they did not respond. It also approached Saint Lucia Prime Minister Philip J Pierre about the fishermen’s disappearance.

“We still consider it a missing persons case, and our own law enforcement are trying their best to see if they can decide what happened. But as far as we’re concerned, the United States have given us no information on that one,” Pierre said.

What makes Joseph and William’s case unique is that police have the remains of their boat – one of the few pieces of physical evidence preserved from the US strikes.

Fault Lines was able to see the wreckage in person, behind a police building, where for months weeds had grown over it. Its team also tracked down the boat’s owner to determine whether it was the vessel Joseph and William had been on board.

Cameron Tayliam, the owner of Zouti Boats, said he was able to recover the remains of the boat before it sank.

He added that he recognised the boat as one of his own by its colours: green on the outside, black on the bottom and red on the inside.

But even with the remnants of the boat, experts say justice may be difficult to come by.

To date, the US government has not published the names of those killed in the boat-bombing campaign, nor has it provided any public evidence to justify the attacks.

Instead, Trump has repeatedly claimed that the boat bombings save lives by preventing illicit drugs from reaching US soil. “Every boat that we knock out, we save 25,000 American lives,” he said last October, without providing proof.

In an unreleased memo obtained by US media, Trump has also claimed the country is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug-trafficking organisations.

The memo directed the US military to “conduct operations” against such groups, despite the fact that Congress has not signed off on such actions.

Amanda Klasing, the national director for government relations and advocacy at Amnesty International USA, is sceptical of Trump’s rationale.

“There is no evidence that the people that are being killed in this campaign have any means by which they could cause harm or violence against Americans. They have no intent to invade the United States,” Klasing said.

Former US Army captain Margaret Donovan, who served as a lawyer in the Judge Advocate General’s (JAG) Corps, also told Fault Lines she sees no apparent legal justification for the boat strikes.

“In order to use lethal force against anybody in a military setting, you need to have congressional authorisation or some [need for] imminent self-defence,” Donovan said.

In cases of self-defence, she explained, “the executive can temporarily authorise lethal force later to be confirmed by the Congress”.

But under international law, drug trafficking is not akin to a military attack. It is also not understood to be justification for an act of lethal self-defence.

It is a crime, and authorities have long addressed the problem by intercepting boats and arresting suspected traffickers.

Trump, however, has argued that such interdiction efforts are ineffective. But experts like Donovan warn that summarily killing people in international waters, without a trial or due process, is illegal.

“If you’re looking at it from a domestic legal perspective, it’s murder. If you’re looking at it from an international legal perspective, it’s a war crime,” said Donovan.

At least two legal challenges are being heard against the boat bombing campaign. One is being led by the families of two Trinidadian men, who disappeared after an October 14 strike. That case is being heard in a US federal court.

The other concerns Alejandro Carranza , a Colombian fisherman who disappeared off the coast of La Guajira on September 15, 2025.

In December, Carranza’s family filed a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, arguing the fisherman’s rights to life and due process had been violated.

Carranza’s friend, Leonardo Vega, saw the video Trump had posted of that day’s strike and connected his disappearance to it.

“We have no doubt. Time has passed, and nothing more was ever heard of Alejandro,” Vega told Fault Lines .

Though Trump identified the victims as “narcoterrorists from Venezuela”, Vega said he knew otherwise. “We, as fishermen, realised it was a Colombian vessel.”

Carranza’s partner, Katerine Hernandez, told Fault Lines his family initially hoped that Carranza had jumped into the water to escape the blast. As time went on, they waited for his body to be found.

“At one point, I wondered whether they could recover even a finger or something, but I don’t know. There is nothing left,” she said.

Hernandez explained that Carranza had called his family before setting sail one last time. She forcefully denies the Trump administration’s accusations of drug trafficking.

“If he really was a narcoterrorist, as they say, why didn’t they pursue him, capture him and prove that he was a narcoterrorist? And if he had been a narcoterrorist, we would have had money, property, an inheritance — something,” Hernandez said.

Fault Lines reached out to the Defense Department, the State Department, the White House and US Southern Command, which oversees military operations in Central and South America, to confirm whether Carranza, Joseph or William were killed in the strikes.

They did not respond to questions about the identities of those killed.

In a written statement, the White House said, “All of these decisive strikes have been against designated narcoterrorists bringing deadly poison to our shores.”

US Southern Command, meanwhile, said it “will not comment on individual cases, including narcoterrorists killed in kinetic strikes”. It also defended the legality of the boat bombing campaign.

“All kinetic strike operations are conducted under strict lawful authority, based on comprehensive intelligence and established targeting criteria,” a spokesperson said.

The strikes, meanwhile, have continued. On August 23, US Southern Command announced that an attack on a “low-profile vessel” killed two people. Two days later, another strike killed four. No victims were identified in any of the cases.

For families, the lack of transparency has brought uncertainty and grief. Relatives who suspect their loved ones may have been killed lack the closure that official confirmation — or a body — can bring.

Charlery feels like the US has taken “a piece” of him. He continues to grapple with the disappearance of his father.

“It’s sad that there is no body to bury,” Charlery says. “Sometimes I wonder if there is justice.”

articles.title: Tillis urges Trump to fire Hegseth over ‘inept management’ of military
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a former member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, is calling on President Trump to fire Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over what he called Hegseth’s “inept management” of the military. Tillis stepped up his criticism of Hegseth’s leadership after Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced his resignation after repeatedly clashing with…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a former member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, is calling on President Trump to fire Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over what he called Hegseth’s “inept management” of the military.

Tillis stepped up his criticism of Hegseth’s leadership after Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced his resignation after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over the ouster of senior officials, such as former Army Chief of Staff Randy George.

Tillis praised Driscoll as “the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians” and vented his anger over Hegseth’s management of the Pentagon.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Tillis posted on X , the social media platform.

Tillis, who cast a pivotal vote to confirm Hegseth last year, is now calling on Trump to fire him.

“I urge the president to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” Tillis said.

He accused Hegseth of “creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks” by pushing an array of senior military officers out of their jobs.

Those officials include Gen. Chris Donahue, the top U.S. Army Commander in Europe; former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. CQ Brown Jr.; Admiral Lisa Franchetti, the Navy’s top officer; Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin; and Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. James Mingus.

Tillis praised Driscoll’s and George’s support for the Army Transformation Initiative, which sought to speed up the deployment of unmanned aircraft systems in Army operations.

“Our understanding and assumptions of warfare are being challenged in places like Ukraine and Iran, and Dan understands the old way of doing business no longer applies. He and General George began a transformative period of innovation in how we array our forces and equip our Soldiers. He challenged our legacy approach to manning and procurement,” Tillis wrote.

“Most of all, he cared deeply about the men and women in our Army formations and quickly earned their respect,” the North Carolina senator added of Driscoll.

Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army’s acting chief of staff, ordered a Europe-based Army battalion to shut down its experimental drone initiative and focus on its core mission as an airborne infantry unit.

Other GOP lawmakers have expressed dismay over Driscoll’s resignation.

“I was disappointed. I think he’s been a pretty solid guy. So disappointed,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said of Discroll’s departure after butting heads with Hegseth over the ouster of key senior officials.

Rounds also cited the development of cutting-edge drone tactics as vital to the future of the Army’s combat readiness.

“This issue that’s going on with regard to Ukraine, the use of drones, the integration of drones into this — this is not a new thing that just happened. We’ve been watching this ever since 2021. … Watching the Ukrainians do a marvelous job with drones. We’ve been watching this,” he said.
